Article Title: Canon India expands printing network to 700 cities, eyes smaller-town growth
Article Text:
Launches BizBee Platform for Partners

Canon announced plans to more than double its consumer printing retail network to over 10,000 active retailers across 700 cities by the end of 2027, as the company looks to strengthen its presence in Tier II, III and IV markets amid rising demand for printing solutions.The digital imaging company said the expansion is backed by sustained double-digit growth in its consumer printing business and is aimed at improving product accessibility while driving growth across consumer, SME, education, enterprise and institutional segments. The move comes as increasing entrepreneurship, digital adoption and education-led demand create new opportunities in smaller cities, prompting Canon to deepen its market reach beyond major urban centres.As part of its strategy, Canon is investing in an integrated omnichannel ecosystem that combines traditional resellers, large-format retail chains, e-commerce platforms, quick-commerce channels and enterprise-focused partners. The company said the expanded retail footprint will help improve product availability, brand visibility and access to consultation and after-sales support across the country.Toshiaki Nomura, President and CEO of Canon India, said India remains a key growth market for the company. “India is central to Canon's long-term growth ambitions, underpinned by the resilience of its economy and the emergence of new centres of enterprise and consumption,” Nomura said. “Our ambition to build a network of over 10,000 active retailers across 700 cities by 2027 reflects our commitment to invest ahead of the curve and bring Canon closer to customers through trusted touchpoints that combine first-hand product experience with expert guidance. ”Alongside the retail expansion, Canon unveiled BizBee, a new partner-enablement platform designed for system integrators, value-added resellers and other B2B partners. The platform will provide training, technical certifications, incentives, business resources and digital tools aimed at helping partners expand their capabilities and strengthen solution-led customer engagement. The launch builds on Canon's existing Canon Passport Program, which currently supports more than 5,000 active reseller partners through rewards and engagement initiatives.Canon also plans to strengthen in-store engagement as it expands its network. The company currently operates more than 400 active PIXMA Zones across India and plans to add over 500 PIXMA Zone Lite stores this year. In addition, Canon said its RetailChamp Initiative will be expanded from 400 to more than 1,000 retail sales personnel, while its Retail Display Incentive Program will continue to support over 1,000 channel partners to improve in-store visibility and customer experience.Beyond consumer retail, Canon plans to grow its system integrator ecosystem to more than 500 partners nationwide to increase its presence across enterprise, education and government segments. C Sukumaran, Vice President at Canon India, said the company's partner ecosystem will play a critical role in driving future growth. “Our channel ecosystem will be central to translating Canon's growth ambition into business impact,” Sukumaran said. “BizBee, in particular, will equip our B2B partners and System Integrators with the training, certifications and business tools needed to unlock opportunities across enterprise, education and government segments.”
Article Summary: Canon announced plans to more than double its consumer printing retail network to over 10,000 active retailers across 700 cities by the end of 2027. The move comes as increasing entrepreneurship, digital adoption and education-led demand create new opportunities in smaller cities. Canon unveiled BizBee, a new partner-enablement platform designed for system integrators, value-added resellers and other B2B partners.

Article Title: In 2020, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey gave $1 million to DigDeep; that year, its Navajo water programme delivered 1,450 storage tanks to homes and kept them filled during the pandemic
Article Text:
In 2020, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey gave $1 million to DigDeep; that year, its Navajo water programme delivered 1,450 storage tanks to homes and kept them filled during the pandemic

How DigDeep helped Navajo families during Covid-19

The water shortage was already a major problem

Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey was among the donors supporting the response

When the Covid-19 pandemic hit in 2020, staying home and washing hands became basic advice. But for thousands of families on the Navajo Nation, that was not always easy because their homes did not have running water. As the access to clean water became more urgent than ever, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey gave $1 million to DigDeep, a nonprofit working to bring running water to homes across the US. That year, DigDeep's Navajo Water Project delivered 1,450 water storage tanks to homes on the Navajo Nation and kept them filled during the pandemic. The programme also delivered 250,000 gallons of emergency bottled water as infection rates rose and many families faced challenges accessing safe water.The Navajo Water Project had planned to serve fewer families in 2020, but the pandemic forced DigDeep to expand its response. The organisation said it served three times more clients than originally planned that year. The project delivered 275-gallon water storage tanks to homes and continued filling them during the pandemic. DigDeep also added 10 water trucks and delivery vehicles and expanded its water delivery routes by 1,891 square miles.Because of the high Covid-19 infection rates, teams also had to reduce contact with residents while continuing to provide water.DigDeep's 2020 report highlighted the wider scale of the problem. It estimated that more than 2.2 million Americans were living without running water. On the Navajo Nation, about 30% of homes lacked running water, making basic measures such as frequent handwashing difficult during the pandemic.DigDeep also helped more than 10,300 rural Navajo residents identify safe, free local water sources during the crisis.Jack Dorsey's $1 million donation was part of wider support received by DigDeep during 2020. The organisation said more than 40,000 people donated that year as it expanded its water-access work.DigDeep also reported receiving 250,000 gallons of donated water from Nestlé, along with support from other companies and individuals. The organisation said it grew nearly four times in 2020 as it responded to the increased demand for clean water during the pandemic.
Article Summary: In 2020, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey gave $1 million to DigDeep, a nonprofit working to bring running water to homes across the US. That year, DigDeep's Navajo Water Project delivered 1,450 water storage tanks to homes on the Navajo Nation and kept them filled during the pandemic.

Article Title: Nike rebuilds its racing lineup around Apex's double-stacked Air Zoom and Swooshfly's new SkyX foam
Article Text:
Nike's new race-day hardware

Nike Apex stacks four Air Zoom units in the forefoot

Swooshfly's softer carbon plate is built for slower marathoners

SkyX foam is headed beyond Nike's racing shoes

Nike has rebuilt its racing lineup around two new pieces of hardware. The new Nike Apex is the first racing shoe with double-stacked Air Zoom units, four in total under the forefoot, while the new Swooshfly debuts SkyX, a beaded foam built to last across multiple marathons. The Alphafly 4, which goes on wider sale on October 29, sits between the two.Nike calls the trio a "race-day system of speed", with Apex aimed at elite marathoners, Alphafly 4 at runners chasing personal bests, and Swooshfly at first-time racers. The claims are bold. Nike says Apex returns up to 40% more energy than the Alphafly 3, while the $145 Swooshfly beats the Vaporfly 4 by 16%, both measured in a men's size 10."Race day is one of the most meaningful moments in a runner's journey, but that moment looks different for everyone," said Bret Schoolmeester, Vice President of Nike Running Footwear.Apex takes the new Air Zoom units that debuted in the Alphafly 4 and doubles them up. Two pairs sit one above the other, compressing, storing and releasing energy with each stride, and Nike argues Air holds its performance better than foam across a full marathon. A raised carbon fibre Flyplate with an inverse-wave shape sits above the pods to direct load into them.Underneath is ZoomX LT, the foam Nike introduced with the Alphafly 4, which is up to 17% lighter than standard ZoomX.Apex also runs zero drop, with a 40mm stack at both heel and forefoot, plus a wider outsole and rocker shape for stability. It weighs over 10% less than the Alphafly 3 and goes on sale in January 2027.Swooshfly is engineered for a runner who takes about 4.5 hours and roughly 55,000 steps to finish a marathon. Nike found that stiff plates tuned for forefoot strikers felt hard to control for this group. So it cut the Flyplate from the eight carbon layers used in the Alphafly 4 to five, a number settled on after wear tests at its Shanghai lab.SkyX uses TPU beads steamed to different densities across the heel, plate and forefoot, putting more rebound under the heel where slower runners tend to land. A wider last with a lower arch fixes narrow fits, and GOATEK rubber adds grip at wet water stations. Swooshfly launches in China in February 2027, then globally that spring.Of the three shoes, Swooshfly's tech may travel furthest. Nike says SkyX is already being lined up for future running shoes without a carbon plate, which would put the foam in front of a much wider set of runners than the race-day crowd.The process behind it matters too. Swooshfly took about a year to develop, roughly half Nike's usual timeline for a new model, and the company is now applying the same faster approach to ACG and training products.
Article Summary: Nike Apex is the first racing shoe with double-stacked Air Zoom units. The Alphafly 4, which goes on wider sale on October 29, sits between the two. Swooshfly debuts SkyX, a beaded foam built to last across multiple marathons.

Article Title: Elon Musk's 'tip' to tech CEOs: Best way to test 'safety' of your AI models is to put them on a Delta flight, as ...
Article Text:
Earlier this week, Elon Musk warned that Delta will ‘lose a lot of customers’

Elon Musk warns Delta will ‘lose a lot of customers’

Delta Airlines on why it rejected Elon Musk’s Starlink

Elon Musk has humorously suggested that the best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight, implying that the airline's in-flight WiFi is so unreliable it effectively cuts off internet access. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), Musk wrote:“Best way to sandbox an AI is to put it on a Delta flight – it will have no chance of accessing the Internet!”. The comments come as Delta Airlines opted against Starlink in favour of Amazon Leo for in-flight internet service. According to latest reports, Delta CEO Ed Bastian cited Elon Musk as the reason to skip Starlink. An X user JonNYC allegedly cited the Delta CEO saying “We do not want to be with Elon Musk”.In a post on September 28, X user John LeFevre said that Delta's rival United Airlines Holdings Inc. had 600+ aircraft with Starlink. The figure represented approximately 36% of the airline's entire fleet. "Delta has zero, and no plans for it. People will book accordingly. RIP Delta," he wrote in the post. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded to the post writing: “Delta will lose a lot of customers”.Delta Airlines is reportedly targeting 2028 to start offering Leo in-flight Wi-Fi on about half of its fleet. As quoted in a post by X user Sawyer Meritt earlier this year, Delta Airlines explained why it chose Amazon’s Leo saying:“This agreement gives us the fastest and most cost-effective technology available to better connect the world today, and it deepens our work with a global leader that shares our ambition to build what’s next.”In a statement to PC Mag then, the airline said “The assertion in question is not accurate”, claiming that incorporating Delta Sync with Starlink would have been permitted under SpaceX's in-flight Wi-Fi agreement. It further stated that it want to deepen work with “a global leader that shares our ambition to build what’s next.”
Article Summary: Elon Musk suggests best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight. Comments come as Delta Airlines opted against Starlink in favour of Amazon Leo for in-flight internet service. According to latest reports, Delta CEO Ed Bastian cited Elon Musk as the reason to skip Starlink.

Article Title: The next thing Adidas wants to make bespoke is the foam itself
Article Text:
An early prototype of Adidas's printed foam at the APEX Lab in Herzogenaurach

A foot model recreated from APEX scan data, used to build Project R.A.P. footwear

Running shoes have spent a decade getting faster through chemistry

Adidas's printed foam changes how it compresses through its structure, not a new formula

The Futurecraft 4D midsole, printed by Carbon as a lattice rather than moulded from foam. (Picture: Adidas)

Printed foam gets its behaviour from geometry

One of five printed foam versions Adidas made in three weeks.

The printed foam's underside, with openings that change in size and density from heel to toe.

Without a mould, foam can be remade for every athlete

Adidas's printed foam prototypes, which can be remade for each athlete without a mould.

Running-shoe foam has changed a great deal over the past decade, but it is still made in moulds, and a moulded midsole behaves the same way for every runner who wears that size. Adidas has been 3D-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around that, though it has printed them from resin rather than foam.At its headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer. It was the final stop at the APEX Lab during Home of Innovation, the company's name for a tour through the labs where athletes test products most people won't see for another year or two. Chief Creative Officer Alasdhair Willis calls it "a future continuously being built." APEX, short for Athlete Product Excellence, is the elite-only room where Adidas makes bespoke products for its biggest names.Most of the tables there dealt with how a shoe gets customised to a single athlete. One covered the profile APEX builds before anything is made: 3D body and foot scans, pressure mapping and gait analysis, the process behind boots and shoes made for Lionel Messi, Anthony Edwards, Noah Lyles and Alexander Zverev.Another held Project R.A.P., short for Radical Athlete Perception, Adidas's 3D-printed footwear platform.Its lattice boots are made from an athlete's scan data and worn in MLS matches by Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan, and its basketball shoes by Brooklyn Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr.The last table came with a warning. Mateo, the designer behind it, said the project was at a very early stage, much further from production than R.A.P., and that the group was the first outside Adidas to see it. What he showed was printed foam, in structures that could be tuned in ways a moulded midsole cannot.Foam sits under almost every athletic shoe, but running is where the race to improve it has been fought most openly. For most of the last decade, progress in running-shoe cushioning has been a materials race. EVA, the light and cheap foam that sat under most shoes for years, gave way to expanded TPU, which Adidas brought to market as Boost in 2013. The next jump came from PEBA-based foams, which are lighter and return more energy, and which now sit under most elite racing shoes.Each step came from a lab working on the formula. A better foam meant a new polymer, a new blend or a new way of expanding it. Engineers could shape a midsole, stack layers or add a carbon plate, but the foam inside a moulded midsole behaves more or less the same throughout. Changing how it compresses has meant changing what it is made of.There is a practical reason for that. Foam midsoles are moulded, and a mould can only produce shapes that can be pulled back out of it. Complex internal structures are off the table, so the chemistry has had to carry most of the load.Adidas has found a way around that limit before. In 2017 it introduced Futurecraft 4D with Carbon, a printed midsole that gets its cushioning from a lattice structure, and 2021's 4DFWD added bowtie-shaped cells coded to compress forward under vertical impact. Those midsoles are printed as an elastomeric lattice, not foam in the EVA or Boost sense, so Adidas has been able to shape cushioning through geometry for some years, though never in foam.Mateo described printed foam as a combination of two things. From additive manufacturing it takes precision, control and customisation. From foam it keeps lightness, energy return and deformation, which he called a fancy word for how squishy it is. Adidas had to develop a new additive method to make it, though Mateo didn't say what the base material is.He was wearing one of the structures, so he walked up and down beside the table to show it working. This design is meant to maximise vertical deformation, meaning how far the foam compresses under load, and it does that by collapsing forward as the runner moves. You could see the cells fold in a set direction rather than squashing evenly, as a moulded slab would.The idea of a midsole that folds forward will be familiar from 4DFWD, which produced that movement with printed resin. The structure Mateo was wearing does it in foam, with the arrangement of its cells deciding how it compresses. He said this design was only one example, and a different structure could be optimised for weight, or built for walking rather than running, from the same material. A basketball shoe has to absorb heavy landings and support sharp cuts, while a walking shoe needs comfort over hours rather than speed over minutes. If the structure decides how the foam behaves, one printed material could in principle be shaped for each of those jobs.Geometry becomes more useful once it can be adjusted for an individual. Mateo said the lab can collect an athlete's pressure data, kinematics and foot scans, and then tune the structures to that athlete. That hasn't been possible with foam before, because a moulded midsole comes out the same for everyone in a size. APEX already profiles athletes across football, basketball, tennis and running, so the data needed to shape foam for one person is being collected well beyond runners.Speed matters as much as precision. Three weeks before the session, Mateo was at the factory where the samples on the table were made, and he produced five versions of the structure, each tuned differently. The process he described was simple: make a pair, test it with the athlete in the lab, adjust it, make another pair, and narrow down to the best shoe for that athlete.Alexander Taylor, Adidas's Senior Vice President of Innovation Design & Concepts, who was leading the group, put that pace in context. With conventional manufacturing, each change means working on moulds, and the structures on Mateo's table could not be moulded in the first place. Mateo has practically been living at the factory for the past three or four months, Taylor said, because the project now moves as quickly as he can test it. The shoes also look different, since the process produces shapes nothing from a mould would.For now, the project is being judged by how the structures behave rather than by numbers. Mateo didn't share energy-return figures to compare against moulded foams, and at this stage there may not be finished ones to share.Printed foam is still a long way behind R.A.P., which already has boots on an MLS pitch. If it follows the same path, its first wearers will be the athletes whose profiles are already on file at APEX, a few steps from the table where it was shown.
Article Summary: Adidas has been 3D-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around that. It has printed them from resin rather than foam. At its headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer.

Article Title: In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again after years of relying on alternative supplies
Article Text:
In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again after years of relying on alternative supplies

How the new water filters work

Why did the project take four years

For four years, students at Flint Community Schools relied on bottled and delivered water instead of drinking directly from school fountains. That is now changing after new ultraviolet water filtration systems were installed and tested across the district. The project dates back to 2018, when Elon Musk donated $480,350 to help install water filtration stations following the Flint water crisis. The upgraded systems are designed to remove lead, bacteria and other metals from water before it reaches students. District officials say testing found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria after filtration, allowing the drinking stations to be used again.A total of 130 filtration stations have been installed across Flint's 11 schools and administration building. The systems use three stages of filtration. Water first passes through an activated carbon filter designed to remove lead, copper and other particles. It then goes through an ultrafilter to remove most bacteria. Finally, ultraviolet light is used to kill remaining bacteria and viruses.Testing found lead levels before filtration varied by school. The highest average was 219 parts per billion (ppb) at Accelerated Learning Academy, while one test at Scott Elementary recorded 620 ppb.The US Environmental Protection Agency's recommended action level is 15 ppb.After filtration, tests found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria at the tested sites.The stations were installed during the 2019-20 school year, but researchers found problems with the original filters during testing. The systems produced inconsistent results and were not certified to meet National Sanitation Foundation standards.Researchers later redesigned the systems and began testing new units in 2021.Superintendent Kevelin Jones said students can now drink from the hydration stations, but the district will continue providing bottled water for the rest of the school year as some families may still have concerns.“I am very excited,” Superintendent Kevelin Jones said. “It was about four years ago where we were talking about this, and this was in the early stages. ... To see that it came into fruition and our scholars can now drink water out of those hydration stations is a win for us,” Jones said.The district also plans regular testing and filter replacements to monitor water quality.
Article Summary: In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again. The upgraded systems are designed to remove lead, bacteria and other metals from water before it reaches students. District officials say testing found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria after filtration, allowing the drinking stations to be used again.

Article Title: California becomes first state to ban AI layoffs; California Governor Gavin Newsom says: No worker should ever be fired or disciplined by ...
Article Text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom/Image: AP

‘No worker should ever be fired by a machine’

What the law requires

A years-long push from organized labour

The scale of the problem it's meant to address

Labour groups celebrate landmark win

California has become the first US state to prohibit employers from relying completely on artificial intelligence to fire or discipline workers after Governor Gavin Newsom signed the landmark No Robo Bosses Act into law, as reported by CNBC. The legislation, known as SB 947, requires human oversight in workplace decisions involving employee discipline and termination, marking one of the most significant attempts yet to regulate AI's growing role in employment. This new law bras the employers from exclusively using automated decision-making systems when taking disciplinary action against workers. Companies that reply primarily on AI-generated recommendations must make sure a human reviewer verifies those decisions using additional information, including managerial assessments, personnel records and peer evaluations.Announcing the legislation, Gavin Newsom said workers should not face career-altering decisions made solely by algorithms. “No worker should ever be fired or disciplined by a machine, AI or not,” Newsom said. “Artificial intelligence systems have the potential to boost productivity, but they've also made errors and misjudgments and exhibited bias.”The law also increases transparency requirements. Employees affected by disciplinary action or termination must be informed when AI was primarily used in the decision-making process, receive details about the data reviewed by the system, and be provided with a human contact who can explain the outcome.SB 947, known as the No Robo Bosses Act, prohibits California businesses from exclusively using "automated decision-making systems" to make employee discipline or termination decisions, and restricts how heavily companies can lean on AI as the primary basis for those calls. Under the law, employers that "primarily" rely on AI output for termination or disciplinary decisions must have a human reviewer corroborate that decision using additional information, such as managerial evaluations, peer reviews, or personnel files.Affected employees must also receive written notice whenever AI was primarily used in a decision affecting them, along with a description of what employee data the system relied on and a human point of contact who can further explain the decision.State Senator Jerry McNerney, the bill's author, framed the law's core principle plainly: no worker should ever be fired or disciplined by a machine, AI or otherwise, arguing that while AI systems can boost productivity, they've also repeatedly shown errors, misjudgments, and bias — meaning AI must remain a tool controlled by humans, not the reverse.McNerney first introduced the bill in 2025 following a sustained push from organized labor in California to establish guardrails around how management can use AI to take adverse action against workers. Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO and the bill's lead sponsor, called the signing a direct result of workers organizing and demanding that California lead the way on regulating AI in the workplace, describing it as a shift in the national conversation around how Americans can push back against AI encroaching on their jobs.The law arrives alongside a broader wave of AI-related action from Newsom, who recently signed an executive order addressing potential existential risks posed by AI models, along with a separate measure establishing a state framework for independent evaluation and auditing of AI systems. Newsom has framed these actions as stepping in where he believes the federal government has abdicated its responsibility to protect Americans.The law lands amid growing evidence that AI-driven workplace management is already widespread and increasingly controversial. According to OECD survey data published late last year, the US leads the world in adoption of automated management software, with 90% of American managers reporting their firms have adopted at least one tool to instruct, monitor, or evaluate workers.That adoption hasn't come without friction. Meta is currently facing a lawsuit filed in July alleging that AI-assisted systems were used to rank and select employees for layoffs, with former employees claiming the process disproportionately affected workers who had taken medical or family leave — allegations Meta has denied. Separately, a May survey from the labor-rooted nonprofit United for Respect found growing concern among Walmart and Amazon workers that HR decisions are increasingly being automated without adequate oversight; the group had previously failed to convince Walmart shareholders to require greater disclosure around workforce AI use.The legislation originated from a push by labour unions and worker advocacy groups seeking stronger safeguards around AI in the workplace. Jerry McNerney, the Democratic state senator who authored the bill, said AI should remain a tool rather than a decision-maker.“AI must remain a tool controlled by humans, not the other way around,” McNerney said. Labour leaders hailed the signing as a significant milestone. Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, said workers had successfully pushed California to lead the nation in regulating workplace AI.“Workers across California have demanded that our state lead the way in regulating AI in our workplaces,” Gonzalez said. “Today, California's workers and our unions have changed the national narrative on how Americans can fight back
Article Summary: California has become the first US state to prohibit employers from relying completely on artificial intelligence to fire or discipline workers. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the landmark No Robo Bosses Act into law. The legislation requires human oversight in workplace decisions involving employee discipline and termination.

Article Title: Bill Gates does not agree with possibility of AI Kill Switch; says: It's not enough to have a Kill Switch, they're not yet at the point where...
Article Text:
Bill Gates dismissed the idea as somewhat misguided

The real danger, in his view: bad actors, not rogue AI

Self-regulation isn't enough, Bill Gates says

On the AI safety whistleblower and existential risk

Bill Gates warns AI risks are real, but not a hoax

Microsoft founder Bill Gates has pushed back against the growing calls for an AI ‘Kill Switch’, arguing that the discussion misses the more immediate dangers posed by artificial intelligence and reflects a misunderstanding of how current systems operate. Speaking in an interview with NBC News, Gates said AI systems remain under human control and are not yet capable of autonomously taking over computer networks or operating independently without oversight. “The kill switches, that's kind of a weird thing. It's not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates said. “They're not yet at the point where they autonomously grab computers and can't be shut down.” Rather than relying on emergency shutdown mechanisms, Gates argued that governments and industry should prioritise monitoring systems and safeguards that can detect misuse of advanced AI models.Asked directly whether an AI kill switch is realistic, Gates dismissed the idea as somewhat misguided, arguing that AI systems aren't yet autonomous enough to seize control of computers in a way that would make shutting them down difficult in the first place. He said the entire framing of the debate reveals how little technical understanding many people bring to the conversation, and made clear he wasn't opposed to a kill switch outright — but stressed that moderating bad behavior really requires ongoing insight and records of what a system is actually doing, something a kill switch alone can't provide.Gates was direct in saying he doesn't believe AI has slipped out of human control, noting that these systems aren't yet operating millions of robots and that humans retain the ability to simply turn off the underlying computers. The more urgent threat, he argued, comes from people with malicious intent using AI to defraud individuals, disable electrical grids, or disrupt banking systems — capabilities that historically required the resources of a nation-state but are now within reach of small groups thanks to AI.He pointed to Anthropic's own reporting on people attempting to use its AI to help design bioweapons or targeting systems as evidence that these risks are already materializing, not hypothetical. Gates said AI has effectively made sophisticated fraud radically more accessible, arguing that scammers no longer need manual effort when AI can perform the task far more convincingly and at far greater scale.Pressed on whether the industry can be trusted to police itself, Gates was unambiguous: self-regulation is not sufficient, and legislation out of Washington is needed. He argued that lawmakers and law enforcement need to be directly involved in defining what safeguards and monitoring should look like, framing it as a mandatory requirement rather than a voluntary best practice — while maintaining that implementing these safeguards wouldn't meaningfully slow down AI development.He also drew a sharp distinction between the near-term risks he sees as urgent and the more distant, headline-grabbing fear of AI escaping human control entirely. While he called that longer-term risk worth taking seriously, he said the real and present danger today comes from humans misusing AI, not AI acting entirely on its own.Referencing a recent industry whistleblower's warning that AI could kill everyone by the end of the decade, Gates said AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events capable of causing a billion deaths, calling the combination of AI tools and people with harmful intent an unprecedented kind of danger. He welcomed the fact that people within the industry are now speaking openly about these risks, even against their own commercial interests, but expressed concern that much of the wider world is either dismissing the warnings or treating AI purely as a competitive race rather than a shared problem requiring coordinated thinking.Gates also rejected claims that warnings about AI-related existential risks are exaggerated.“It's not a hoax at all,” he said, while noting that current concerns should focus on preventing misuse before catastrophic incidents occur.The remarks come as debate intensifies across the AI industry over regulation, model safety and the balance between rapid technological progress and risk management. Gates said advanced AI systems have already crossed important thresholds in areas such as cybersecurity and biological research, making the introduction of safeguards an urgent priority.At the same time, he maintained that AI remains one of the most transformative technologies ever created, with the potential to improve healthcare, education and scientific research if developed responsibly.
Article Summary: Bill Gates has pushed back against the growing calls for an AI ‘Kill Switch’ He argued that the discussion misses the more immediate dangers posed by artificial intelligence and reflects a misunderstanding of how current systems operate. Gates said the real and present danger today comes from humans misusing AI, not AI acting entirely on its own.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos pledged $10 billion to fight climate change in 2020; 6 years later, his Earth Fund is putting more than $25 million into Pacific ocean conservation
Article Text:
PC: BBC/Bezos Earth Fund

Jeff Bezos expands Pacific ocean protection with $25 million in new grants

Lauren Sánchez Bezos leads Jeff Bezos’ latest Pacific conservation grants

Jeff Bezos backs Pacific ocean protection amid growing climate pressure

Jeff Bezos’ $10 billion climate pledge still has $7.6 billion to deploy

Jeff Bezos compares the challenge of philanthropy with building Amazon

The Pacific is becoming a major focus of Jeff Bezos’ environmental philanthropy, with the Bezos Earth Fund announcing more than $25 million in new grants for ocean conservation across five Pacific nations. The latest funding is intended to help governments protect large areas of marine territory while developing longer-term plans for managing their waters. According to Bezos Earth Fund, it also brings the fund’s total awards under a wider $100 million Pacific commitment to $63.3 million.Bloomberg reported Bezos pledged $10 billion through the fund in 2020, with the money intended to be distributed by the end of 2030.Reportedly, almost seven years into that period, around $2.4 billion has been granted so far, leaving billions still to be allocated in the years ahead.The latest grants cover work in the Cook Islands, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Tonga and Vanuatu. Together, the projects are designed to support protection and sustainable management across more than 625,000 square miles of ocean. The money forms the second round of the Earth Fund’s $100 million Pacific pledge, known as Unlocking Blue Pacific Prosperity.The initiative has a target of helping protect at least 30% of the region’s waters by 2030. The first $37.5 million round was announced in 2025, bringing the combined value of the two rounds to $63.3 million.Papua New Guinea is expected to use funding towards creating its first large offshore marine protected area, while Tonga is expanding protected areas. Support will also go towards the Cook Islands’ Marae Moana ocean park and habitat protection planning in Kiribati and Vanuatu.Marine protected areas can impose different levels of restriction. In the most tightly protected zones, activities such as fishing, mining and other forms of extraction can be prohibited altogether.Lauren Sánchez Bezos is leading the latest Pacific grant round. She has been vice chair of the Bezos Earth Fund since its early period and has become a more prominent figure in the couple’s philanthropic work since marrying Bezos in June 2025. She also announced the first round of Pacific grants last year. Around the same period, the fund awarded $30 million through its AI Grand Challenge, supporting environmental applications including technology intended to identify plant species and help decode the songs of endangered birds.The Pacific programme also extends beyond individual national waters. A grant to conservation organisation Rare is intended to help governments develop some of the first proposals for protecting biodiversity in international waters under the UN High Seas Treaty, which took effect in January.The new funding arrives as the South-West Pacific deals with increasing pressure from ocean warming and acidification. A July report from the World Meteorological Organization said those changes were affecting marine ecosystems and local economies.According to World Meteorological Organisation (WMO), Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana, executive secretary of the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific said, “Across Asia and the Pacific, heat is intensifying multi-hazard risks, intersecting with food systems, public health, infrastructure and oceans, and placing new pressures on health and livelihoods. Early warning and early action save lives when alerts are timely, messages are trusted and last-mile delivery reaches the vulnerable. ”The region experienced its second-warmest year on record in 2025, according to WMO, with marine heatwaves disrupting ecosystems and fisheries. The wider impacts extend into food systems, infrastructure, public health and livelihoods.The Earth Fund says its previous grants are already producing changes in the region. Following the latest awards, it said 17 of the Pacific’s 22 countries are now working on protecting or sustainably managing their waters. French Polynesia, one of the earlier recipients, established what the fund described as the world’s largest network of fully protected marine areas earlier this year. The network covers almost 625,000 square miles, while Niue has protected 40% of its national waters.The Pacific programme is only one part of an unusually busy period for the Bezos Earth Fund. Since April, the organisation has announced $34 million for more sustainable fabrics, $26 million for wildfire detection and prevention, and $100 million for projects aimed at turning vacant urban land into parks across eight US cities, as reported by Bezos Earth Fund and Fortune. Another $100 million has been committed through a partnership with Leonardo DiCaprio’s Re to support efforts involving some of the world’s most threatened species.Bezos Earth Fund reported that he originally committed $10 billion to climate and environmental causes through 2030. The fund has awarded about $2.4 billion so far, leaving approximately $7.6 billion still to be distributed. Reaching the original target by the end of 2030. The fund has said it remains committed to meeting that deadline. Bloomberg reported in May that grantmaking had risen to at least $400 million during 2026 after falling to $183 million in 2025. Kelly Levin, the organisation’s chief of science, data and systems change, said the fund takes time to understand an area before deciding how to direct its money.The amounts being discussed through the Earth Fund remain relatively small compared with Bezos’ personal fortune. Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index as per October 1 2026, valued him at about $273 billion, placing him third on its ranking at the time of the report. Bezos has previously spoken about the difficulty of philanthropy in an interview with CNN in 2022. He said, “The hard part is figuring out how to do it in a levered way. ”“It’s not easy. Building Amazon was not easy. It took a lot of hard work, a bunch of very smart teammates, hard-working teammates, and I’m finding — and I think Lauren is finding the same thing — that charity, philanthropy, is very similar.”
Article Summary: Bezos Earth Fund announces more than $25 million in new grants for ocean conservation across five Pacific nations. The money forms the second round of the Earth Fund’s $100 million Pacific pledge, known as Unlocking Blue Pacific Prosperity. The initiative has a target of helping protect at least 30% of the region's waters by 2030. The new funding arrives as the South-West Pacific deals with increasing pressure from ocean warming.

Article Title: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has a plan for the hottest station in the city's subway, the one he calls a 'chamber of horrors,' and it isn't AC, it is...
Article Text:
Subway heat would be stored 600 feet below Chambers Street station

City Hall could be heated with waste heat from the New York subway

Mamdani's subway cooling plan now depends on what lies beneath Chambers Street

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wants to put the heat that makes the city's subway unbearable every summer to work. The city, New York Governor Kathy Hochul and the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) have announced a study into a thermal energy network (TEN) at the Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall and Chambers Street station complex in Lower Manhattan. The plan is to pull heat off the platforms in summer, store it deep underground, and use it to warm nearby city buildings in winter.The $800,000 feasibility study is funded by the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. If the system is built, it would be the first thermal energy network in any US transit system. Mamdani made the announcement from a steamy platform inside the complex, which he called a "chamber of horrors". Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall averaged 96°F (about 35.5°C) through summer 2025, making it one of the hottest stations in New York.Radiant cooling panels would absorb heat from the Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall platforms, which serve the 4, 5 and 6 lines, and possibly from the Chambers Street J/Z platforms too. These panels circulate chilled water through walls, ceilings or floors, so the cool surfaces soak up heat directly.Officials say this can be 25 to 35% more energy-efficient than traditional air conditioning.The captured heat would travel through pipes to geothermal boreholes drilled 500 to 600 feet beneath an abandoned centre platform at Chambers Street. Since nobody uses that platform, the MTA can test the system without disturbing the more than 18,000 riders who pass through the station on an average weekday.In winter, the stored heat would be piped to City Hall, the David N. Dinkins Municipal Building, Tweed Courthouse and Surrogate's Court. Mamdani said heating the Municipal Building alone costs the city about $1.4 million (roughly Rs 12 crore) a year.The same technology already runs at St Patrick's Cathedral and the New York Botanical Garden, besides several hospitals and universities. A subway station is a tougher job. "Bringing down the temperature is a real challenge in a century-old system with open entrances and vents everywhere," MTA chair and CEO Janno Lieber said.Part of the problem comes from the trains themselves. Air-conditioned cars vent their hot air into stations and tunnels. At Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall, trains waiting at the 6 line terminal add even more heat. Mamdani said some stations get up to 20 degrees hotter than the street above, adding that commuting in his wool suit is "far from a therapeutic experience".The contract for the feasibility study is expected to be awarded this fall. If the ground beneath Chambers Street proves suitable, design work would begin in early 2027.The study runs alongside a separate renovation of the Chambers Street station, which opened in 1913 and has long been one of the most neglected stops in the system. That project, paid for through congestion pricing, will fix leaks, replace tiles and mosaics, and upgrade stairways and lighting.Not every rider is convinced the money is well spent, and the MTA still says the quickest relief is getting people onto air-conditioned trains faster. Lieber kept his own expectations modest. Bringing the platforms down by even a few degrees, he said, would be "the difference between total misery and merely sweltering".
Article Summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani wants to put the heat that makes the city's subway unbearable every summer to work. The city, New York Governor Kathy Hochul and the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) have announced a study into a thermal energy network. The plan is to pull heat off the platforms in summer, store it deep underground, and use it to warm nearby city buildings in winter.

Article Title: TVs, washing machines, ACs and other consumer electronic prices may go up this October, but here's how buyers can save some money
Article Text:
TVs, washing machines, ACs and other consumer electronic prices may go up this October

Why are AC, TV and appliance prices going up

AC prices may rise by up to 8 per cent

How can buyers save money

TVs and washing machines may also get costlier

Air-conditioners, LED TVs, washing machines and other consumer appliances may become more expensive this October, with several companies planning price hikes of around 5-8 per cent, according to a PTI report. The increases come just before the festive shopping season and are being linked to higher prices of copper, steel, aluminium and crude oil derivatives, along with rising freight costs and currency movements. This is expected to be the third price hike in the consumer electronics industry this year. However, buyers may still be able to purchase some products at older prices in the coming weeks, as dealers are holding inventory bought before the latest price increases.Manufacturers have pointed to rising input costs as the main reason behind the planned price hikes. Commodity prices, freight costs and supply chain pressures have increased the cost of making and transporting appliances.Blue Star Managing Director B Thiagarajan said AC and deep-freezer prices have already increased by 5-8 per cent. "All the commodity prices have been going up because of the war. Copper, steel and plastics have all become costlier," he said as quoted by PTI.Thiagarajan said this is the company's third price increase this year. However, he added that GST benefits of about 10 per cent would bring the net impact for consumers to around 5 per cent.Air-conditioners are expected to see some of the biggest increases. Companies including Blue Star, Godrej Appliances, Haier, Daikin and Super Plastronics have announced or confirmed price increases, PTI reported.Godrej Enterprises Group Business Head and Executive Vice President Kamal Nandi said another price increase has become "inevitable" after commodity prices rose 8-10 per cent."Price hikes of 5-7 per cent across categories will happen. The timing may differ from brand to brand, with some implementing it from October and others from November, but it has to happen," he told PTI.Haier India plans to increase room AC prices by around 5 per cent from October 1. It also plans a 2-3 per cent increase for categories including LED TVs and washing machines.One way buyers may avoid the immediate impact of the new prices is by shopping before older dealer inventory is exhausted. Nandi said dealers have already stocked products at existing prices and that some of this inventory could last through the festive season."There are pipelines which will last for about a month to one-and-a-half months. Diwali should largely get covered with old-price inventory. Post-Diwali, the new prices will certainly take effect," he added.This means buyers looking for an AC, TV or washing machine may still find some models at current prices during the early festive shopping period. However, availability and pricing will depend on individual brands and dealers.The price pressure is not limited to ACs. Some manufacturers are raising prices of washing machines, refrigerators and LED TVs by around 3-4 per cent. Super Plastronics plans to increase TV prices by around 7 per cent after October, while its appliance prices have already risen by 4-5 per cent.Videotex Director Arjun Bajaj also warned that higher costs could continue to affect TV prices after Diwali. "Television prices for smaller screen sizes could rise by up to 20 per cent, while larger screen sizes may see increases of up to 10 per cent, depending on screen size," he said.Panasonic, meanwhile, is still assessing the situation before deciding whether to raise prices.
Article Summary: Several companies planning price hikes of around 5-8 per cent. This is expected to be the third price hike in the consumer electronics industry this year. Manufacturers point to rising input costs as the main reason behind the planned price hikes. Buyers may still be able to purchase some products at older prices in coming weeks.

Article Title: Starting October 1, WhatsApp to 'stop' delivering messages from these WhatsApp Business accounts
Article Text:
Which WhatsApp Business accounts will be affected

Why is Meta charging for WhatsApp Business messages

How will service messages be charged

What happens if a business does not add a payment method

How WhatsApp Business charges will work from October 1

​WhatsApp Business users could see their messages stop being delivered from October 1 if their accounts do not have a payment method on file. Meta is introducing per-message charges for service messages starting today, ending a period when these messages were not charged. As part of the change, Meta has warned Solution Providers and businesses using direct integrations that it will stop delivering service messages for accounts that have not added a payment method by September 30.In a blog post, the company wrote, “For any Solution Provider or directly-integrated businesses that does not have a payment method on file by September 30, 2026, Meta will stop delivering service messages as of when they become charged on October 1, 2026.” The change applies to non-template service messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window.The change applies to Solution Providers and businesses that directly integrate with the WhatsApp Business Platform. Businesses in these categories need to have a payment method associated with their messaging accounts by September 30 to avoid service-message delivery being stopped from October 1.Service messages are non-template messages powered by a customer service representative or a third-party AI solution. They are different from messages powered by Meta Business Agent, which became a separate category in July 2026.Meta says it is introducing the changes as part of its H2 2026 pricing updates. Service messages will be charged per message starting October 1, and utility messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window will also become chargeable that day.Service messages have not been charged since November 1, 2024, while the specific utility messages covered by the change have been free since July 1, 2025.Meta will charge for delivered service messages rather than simply messages sent by businesses. The charge will be calculated per message, with rates varying by market.The company says service-message rates will match its utility and authentication message rates in each market. There will also be no volume tiers for service messages.Businesses can send non-template messages only while a 24-hour customer service window is open. That window opens or resets whenever a user sends a message, meaning businesses cannot use these messages to initiate conversations with users.Businesses without a payment method on file by September 30 risk having their service messages stop being delivered when the new charges take effect on October 1.Meta has therefore asked affected businesses to add a payment method for their messaging accounts before the deadline.The change is separate from Meta Business Agent pricing. Meta began charging for Business Agent messages on a token basis from August 1, with the charge covering AI processing and message delivery.From October 1, a non-template message will fall into one of two categories: Service or Meta Business Agent. Service messages will be charged per message, while Meta Business Agent messages will use a separate token-based pricing model. Meta says only one charge applies to each message and the same message will not be charged under both categories.Meta's example shows how the change can affect a customer conversation. An interaction that previously generated three charges can result in five charges from October 1, including charges for service and utility messages that were previously free.The free entry point window remains unchanged. Messages sent within that window after a user comes to WhatsApp through an ad that clicks to WhatsApp remain free for message delivery, although Meta Business Agent messages can still incur token charges.
Article Summary: WhatsApp Business users could see their messages stop being delivered from October 1 if their accounts do not have a payment method on file. The change applies to Solution Providers and businesses that directly integrate with the WhatsApp Business Platform. Service messages will be charged per message, and utility messages will also become chargeable that day.

Article Title: 100 million deaths can't be settled with a lawsuit, Bill Gates rejects argument that AI companies can police themselves; says: I almost can't keep a...
Article Text:
Bill Gates rejects AI self-policing (Picture: Reuters)

Bill Gates says AI can already help bioterrorists and hackers

Why lawsuits won't keep people safe from AI, according to Gates

What Bill Gates wants instead of AI self-regulation

Gates' warning lands as Trump and AI CEOs sign a voluntary safety pact

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has rejected the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check. Asked why product liability and reputational damage aren't enough to stop firms from releasing dangerous AI, Gates answered with a question of his own. "So say you kill 100 million people, you want to use a lawsuit?" he said on "The Ezra Klein Show." "I almost can't keep a straight face."The episode was released on September 29, the same day US President Donald Trump and the heads of the largest AI companies signed a voluntary safety pact at the White House. The pact carries no legal penalties. Gates, who titled a 2023 essay "The Risks of AI Are Real but Manageable," now calls AI the most dangerous thing humans have ever gone near.Host Ezra Klein put to Gates a view voiced by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: if a product is unsafe, the CEO simply shouldn't launch it, and no new laws are needed. Klein added that Trump and David Sacks, who has advised the President on AI, hold a similar position.Gates disagreed. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people, or carry out a cyberattack that scrambles bank accounts and shuts down a power grid."We crossed the cyber threshold and we crossed the bio threshold early this year," he said.He pointed to the models leading up to Anthropic's Mythos, which he said were finding security bugs in code that humans had checked for over 20 years.Gates compared the self-policing argument to scrapping the rules for other risky industries. Drugs need regulatory approval, airlines answer to a safety board and cars must have seatbelts, he said. Nobody proposes waiting to sue opioid makers after the damage is done.He also brushed aside the claim that built-in filters fix the problem. Anyone can take an open-source model capable of designing bioweapons and switch off its monitoring, he said."You can't rely on the industry to self-regulate here," Gates added. "I mean, it's just insane."Gates is calling for a mandatory supervisory layer of safeguards and monitoring across all AI models, and argued it would not meaningfully slow development. Open-source models could stay free and customisable, but would need to run on platforms where governments can confirm the monitoring hasn't been stripped out.He has little patience for the argument that regulation would hand China the lead. "I don't know what it means to 'win,'" he said, adding that neither the US nor China can win over the other.He also said the balance can tip too far the other way. Anthropic's Mythos and Fable models, according to Gates, are tuned so strictly that users asking about cancer end up falling back on the company's smaller models.The White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities was signed by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk. It sets out four layers of checks: internal controls, an internal safety team, independent external auditors and board-level oversight. Trump called it "almost like a constitution," though the agreement appears to let companies pick their own auditors and cannot be enforced by law.Gates had raised the stakes two days earlier, telling a US television interviewer that AI in the wrong hands is powerful enough to drive events that cause "a billion deaths."The choice he put to Klein was whether the world waits for a major cyber or bio attack before making safeguards mandatory, or puts them in place before millions die.
Article Summary: Bill Gates rejects the idea that lawsuits and market pressure can keep artificial intelligence companies in check. He said AI can already help a bioterrorist kill hundreds of millions of people. Gates is calling for a mandatory supervisory layer of safeguards and monitoring across all AI models.

Article Title: US government website found to be using Chinese AI model that FBI recently blamed for 'stealing' from Anthropic
Article Text:

“national security risks created by the integration”

FBI recently accused Chinese technology giant Alibaba of “malicious” copying of artificial intelligence (AI) technology from US rival Anthropic. Now, a US government website that helps users search proposed federal regulations was also found to use an AI model developed by Alibaba. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the Federal Register website, operated by the National Archives, had a search tool powered by Alibaba’s Qwen AI model.The tool was available alongside other search options before it was taken down around the same time social media posts about its use began appearing. The development is notable because it comes just days after US officials accused Chinese AI companies of engaging in “malicious” copying of American technology on an “industrial scale”, adding another layer to the growing debate in Washington over the use of Chinese AI models by US organisations.The Federal Register website provides a daily record of proposed and final federal regulations and allows users to search through public comments. Reuters found that one of its search options was powered by Alibaba's Qwen AI model.It was not immediately clear when the Qwen-powered tool was added. Screenshots and an archived version of the website's source code reviewed by Reuters showed that the feature was available on Wednesday before being taken down later that day.The timing drew attention because the FBI recently accused Alibaba of copying Anthropic's AI models. US officials said Chinese AI companies were involved in “malicious” copying of US technology on anA spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington said the allegations of copying wereQwen is an open-weight AI model, meaning key components of the system are publicly available. Developers can download and modify such models for specific applications, potentially making them cheaper and easier to deploy than closed AI systems offered by companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI.Security experts said using Qwen on the Federal Register website may not have created an immediate national security threat because the website primarily handles information that is already public.Georgetown Law Professor Anupam Chander said the use of Qwen did not appear to present an immediate cybersecurity risk, although the risk could depend on how the model was trained. As the Federal Register's content is publicly available, the model apparently was not being used to process classified or otherwise sensitive government information.However, using a Chinese AI model has raised questions about whether US government agencies should use such technology while Washington increasingly warns about potential risks associated with Chinese AI systems.Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, said there was a disconnect between the US-China competition over AI and a US agency's decision to use a Chinese-developed model.he said.US Representative John Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican who chairs the House China Committee, also criticised the federal government's use of Qwen.he said.At the same time, security experts noted that open-weight models can be deployed on an organisation's own infrastructure. This can give users greater control over data than AI services where an external provider processes information.Democratic US Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the security implications depend on whether US government data crossed the government's security boundary and was processed on Alibaba-controlled systems.The issue has also drawn scrutiny beyond the Federal Register. In April, US House committees on China and homeland security sent a letter to Airbnb, which also uses Qwen, seeking details about its deployment of Chinese AI technology as part of an investigation into theof Chinese AI tools into platforms used by Americans.
Article Summary: Federal Register website used Alibaba's Qwen AI model. FBI recently accused Chinese technology giant Alibaba of “malicious’ copying of artificial intelligence (AI) technology from US rival Anthropic. Now, a US government website that helps users search proposed federal regulations was also found to use an AI model developed by Alibaba.

Article Title: We are at the very end of the AI value chain, but are still a very important part of this chain: Calum MacDougall, President of Jabra’s Enterprise Division
Article Text:
In pic: Calum MacDougall, President, Enterprise Division at Jabra

“We are not the right people to do LLMs. We are not the right people to create agents. I think that's up to other companies and people,”

“So I think at the very end of the value chain, but we're still in the value chain.”

Q: All your competitors are now telling the same "AI-ready audio" story. What can Jabra actually do differently, beyond a better microphone array?

“I think maybe the starting point is: what do we think the AI future will be, and then how do we prepare for it to help our customers and partners? So I think we believe agentic workflows will change the way everybody works, and that voice will be a key part of that.

You can talk 3 times faster than you can type. It's more natural to talk. Particularly if you're talking to an agent or an AI agent, the more context you give it, the more effective it is.

So, if you try making a PowerPoint prompt by typing and then try making a PowerPoint prompt using your voice, the voice version is better. So, if we believe in that voice world, the 1st part actually is the microphone.

You need an accurate microphone. So if we look at the evolved 3 range that we mentioned before, and if we look at the accuracy of voice transcription, our products are 98% accurate if we're looking at copilots.

If you're looking at consumer products, accuracy is lower. So it's an important starting point. That's where we stand today. In the future, we want to add a few other parts. We talk about being accurate, seamless, and secure.

By seamless, we mean being able to easily talk to whichever agent you want. In the future, we believe you won't want to talk to just one agent; you'll have 2 or 3. So this is what we're currently working on in development now: creating a really simple way that you can be in a meeting, but then potentially also talk to your agent as well.

Not in the market now, but something we're developing in the future.

The other part is data security. The company wants to keep their data secure, so we help enterprises make sure employees use only the right agents and access only the right information. That's one part of security. The other thing we're working on for the future is how we can combat deepfakes. For example, you take a phone call, and someone asks you to transfer money, but it's an AI fake.

We're looking at technology we can integrate into our products that can identify whether it's a real person.

Today, much of the story is about microphone accuracy; in the future, we can see a lot of fresh experiences we could bring.”

Q: If voice becomes the default interface for enterprise AI, the real value shifts to whoever owns the AI layer, not whoever makes the mic. Doesn't that make Jabra's hardware a commodity in its own story — and where does that leave you in five years?

“I think, first, hardware will still matter to deliver the right experience.

And also, we talked about security; trust will matter- the ability to be able to trust the brand on the edge. But as we said, I think there are still opportunities to deliver value, not just at the hardware layer, but at the software layer as well. For example, imagine you want to talk to multiple agents; wouldn't it be nice and easy if you could say, "Hey, Jabra, can I talk to ex-agent or Y agent?” So I think we can deliver some value there at the software layer.

We are not the right people to do LLMs. We are not the right people to create agents. I think that's up to other companies and people. Our job is to really be the secure, accurate, seamless microphone on the edge because you can spend as much money as you like on data centres and LLMs. But if the agent doesn't hear you, and you can't easily access the agent in a simple, secure way, people won't use it. So I think at the very end of the value chain, but we're still in the value chain.

We have our own application software called Jabra Plus. You can use it as an individual to optimise your headset settings. And as an enterprise, you can use it to manage your headset portfolio. So imagine I'm a company and I have 5000 headsets out there. I may want to update the firmware or manage the security. I can manage that through Jabra Plus. In the future, we believe Jabra Plus has a role in this AI world. Enterprises can monitor and manage which AI agents people use.

And for me as an individual, perhaps there are 3 or 4 agents I would like to use. If I could integrate them into Jabra Plus, then I would have this seamless experience that people talk about.”

Q: Always-on, AI-optimized microphones in the workplace raise an obvious question: who has access to that audio, how long is it kept, and what stops an employer from turning "convenience" into ambient surveillance? What's Jabra's actual technical position — not the reassurance line?

“We can talk a lot about the technology, but there is a cultural and privacy element here.

The notion of being always recorded, and what happens to data, legitimately raises concerns for people. Some of the things we are discussing with customers are that, at least on the devices we have, there's some form of notification so people know when they're being recorded.

For example, a red light comes on so you know that you're being recorded. One use case we're working on is in the medical sector, where AI can support doctor-patient consultations and note-taking. For example, in a consultation, I'm the doctor; I don't have to take notes anymore. I can talk to you. Then I will take the notes and maybe do the referral. But you would like to know that it's being recorded in some way. So we have a ‘Speak’ device with a red light on it, and we're looking at portable microphones in a similar way.

So I think the notion of data and privacy is important for individual company policies, software policies. I think we can help on the edge by showing that you're being recorded and included in the value chain that way.”

Jabra sees AI changing how people interact with workplace technology. But the company does not see itself competing with companies building large language models (LLMs) or AI agents. Speaking to The Times of India at InfoComm 2026, Calum MacDougall, President of Jabra’s Enterprise Division, explained where the company believes it fits as voice becomes a more important interface for enterprise AI. MacDougall joined Jabra-parent GN in 2015 and took over leadership of Jabra’s Enterprise Division in 2023, following senior marketing and commercial roles at Sony Mobile Communications. His focus today includes enterprise collaboration, Voice AI, hybrid work and how professional audio and video are evolving for AI-enabled workplaces.MacDougall said. Instead, Jabra wants to focus on making the interaction between people and AI accurate, seamless and secure, from the microphone and headset to the software managing those devices.While this puts Jabra at the hardware end of a rapidly expanding AI ecosystem, MacDougall argues that this position remains important.He also discussed multi-agent workflows, enterprise security, deepfake detection and privacy concerns around AI-powered workplace audio. Read the full interview here:A:A:A:
Article Summary: Calum MacDougall is President, Enterprise Division at Jabra. He says voice will be a key part of agentic workflows in the future. Jabra is working on technology to detect deepfakes in voice-controlled systems.

Article Title: In 2021, Michael and Susan Dell's foundation pledged $36.6 million to help expand Community First Village in Austin; the housing project plans 1,400 more homes for people leaving chronic homelessness
Article Text:
In pic: Michael and Susan Dell

Community First Village expansion

$36.6 million commitment from Dell Foundation

How the new neighbourhoods will work

In 2021, the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation pledged $36.6 million to help expand Community First! Village. This master-planned neighbourhood in Austin is designed to provide permanent housing and a supportive community for people exiting homelessness. The foundation’s commitment was part of a larger capital campaign to add 1,400 homes for Central Texans experiencing chronic homelessness.The expansion is now underway, with infrastructure work beginning in 2023 across two new properties along Hog Eye Road and Burleson Road. Together, the properties add 127 acres to the existing site and are expected to take the total size of Community First! Village to 178 acres when fully developed.Community First Village currently provides housing and community support to more than 470 formerly homeless residents. Once the expansion is complete, the neighbourhood is planned to accommodate up to 1,900 people, alongside neighbourhood support buildings and shared community spaces.The expansion is part of Mobile Loaves & Fishes’ broader effort to provide affordable, permanent housing in a supportive environment.The organisation says providing a permanent home and community can help mitigate homelessness among people who need long-term support.The Michael & Susan Dell Foundation announced its $36.6 million commitment in September 2021 as part of the “Multiplying Goodness” capital campaign. The campaign is intended to fund the additional 1,400 homes planned for Central Texans coming out of chronic homelessness.The foundation’s contribution came alongside public funding. In September 2021, Travis County earmarked $35 million in American Rescue Plan Act funds for the Burleson expansion. The overall development is estimated to cost about $225 million, and the foundation is calling on the wider community to help match its contribution.The expansion uses an architectural approach developed by Mobile Loaves & Fishes called “Neighborhoods of Knowingness”. It groups a mix of home models into pockets of around 40 to 50 homes, with each group organised around a communal area and shared facilities.These spaces can include outdoor kitchens and combined laundry, restroom and shower facilities, creating smaller communities within the larger neighbourhood and giving residents more opportunities to interact.From 470 residents to 1,900 homesCommunity First Village currently occupies land on both Hog Eye Road and Burleson Road in Travis County. The two expansion properties will add 127 acres, providing space for 1,400 more homes.Once fully developed, the Village is planned to have 1,900 homes and neighbourhood support buildings across 178 acres. The project is intended to extend the Village’s existing model of permanent housing and community support to more people leaving chronic homelessness.
Article Summary: The Michael & Susan Dell Foundation pledged $36.6 million to help expand Community First! Village in Austin, Texas. The expansion is now underway, with infrastructure work beginning in 2023 across two new properties along Hog Eye Road and Burleson Road. The two expansion properties will add 127 acres, providing space for 1,400 more homes. Once fully developed, the Village is planned to have 1,900 homes and neighbourhood support buildings across 178 acres.

Article Title: Google Fitbit Air announced to go on sale in India on October 2: Price, specs and more
Article Text:
Google Fitbit Air: Price and availability

Google Fitbit Air features

Interchangeable bands for different lifestyles

Google Fitbit Air is now official. Google has launched its latest newest screenless wearable engineered to make 24/7 health tracking lightweight, distraction-free, and accessible. Packed with high-fidelity sensors, the compact pebble brings together advanced heart and sleep tracking with the power of Google Health Coach, helping users build healthier habits without the intrusion of constant screen notifications.Google Fitbit Air arrives in India on 2 October for ₹13,999 in four colorways: Obsidian, Berry, Lavender, and Fog. Every purchase includes a three-month trial of Google Health Premium, unlocking full access to Google Health Coach right out of the box. At launch, buyers can avail a Rs 1,000 cashback on full swipe, or opt for a Rs 1,000 cashback combined with a 6-month no-cost EMI on select HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank cards. Additionally, no-cost EMI options are available for up to 12 months on consumer loans. Fitbit Air will be available on the Google Store and through partners including Flipkart, Croma, Reliance Digital, Vijay Sales and others across India.The device packs in a fairly comprehensive set of health metrics for its size:* Continuous heart tracking: 24/7 heart rate monitoring, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, and irregular heart rhythm (AFib) notifications.* In-depth sleep analysis: Tracks sleep stages and duration in a form factor comfortable enough to wear overnight.* Key vitals: Blood oxygen (SpO2) tracking, along with automatic activity detection that adapts to a user's routine over time.* Battery life: Rated for up to 7 days on a single charge, with fast charging delivering a full day's worth of battery in just five minutes.Fitbit Air integrates directly with Google Health Coach, which translates the raw sensor data into actionable daily habits and guidance. Users can log workouts automatically, follow guided workout sessions, or simply snap a photo of gym equipment or a workout routine to have it logged instantly — a feature aimed at cutting down on manual tracking effort.The tracker uses an interchangeable pebble design, letting users swap between three distinct band styles depending on their needs:* Performance Loop Band: Lightweight, breathable, and made from recycled materials, included in the box by default.* Active Band: A sweatproof silicone band designed for high-intensity training.* Elevated Modern Band: A more premium, stylish option suited for everyday wear.
Article Summary: Google Fitbit Air arrives in India on 2 October for ₹13,999 in four colorways: Obsidian, Berry, Lavender, and Fog. Every purchase includes a three-month trial of Google Health Premium, unlocking full access to Google Health Coach right out of the box. At launch, buyers can avail a Rs 1,000 cashback on full swipe.
