Article Title: As AI fears ‘spread’, Donald Trump to meet CEOs of Meta, Google, Nvidia, Anthropic and other tech companies
Article Text:
In pic: US President Donald Trump

Donald Trump to meet AI and technology CEOs

Why AI safety is being discussed

What the White House meeting could discuss

Mark Zuckerberg has opposed calls to slow AI development

Donald Trump has rejected calls for AI regulation

“taking over the World”

“destroying Humanity”

“HOAX.”

US President Donald Trump is set to meet the CEOs of several major technology and artificial intelligence companies at the White House. This meeting comes as concerns about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI systems continue to grow. The meeting comes as AI companies, lawmakers and governments debate how rapidly the technology should develop and what safeguards may be needed. A report claims that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are expected to attend the lunch meeting, along with Palantir CEO Alex Karp.According to a report by ABC News, US House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is also expected to attend, has said there should be a “deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play in that.” At the same time, Johnson has opposed a moratorium on AI development, saying the US cannot risk losing its technological edge to China.The White House meeting is expected to bring together executives from some of the world's biggest AI and technology companies at a time when questions over AI safety and regulation are becoming increasingly prominent.Zuckerberg, Amodei, Pichai and Huang are expected to attend, while Karp is also expected to be present.The meeting will be held at the White House with Trump and Johnson.The gathering follows several recent meetings between Trump and technology executives. Zuckerberg, along with CEOs including Sam Altman, Huang, Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and AMD CEO Lisa Su, attended a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping last week. The White House has also previously brought technology leaders together to discuss AI development and US competitiveness.The latest meeting comes amid disagreements over how governments and technology companies should respond as AI models become more capable.Johnson previously said the White House meeting would focus on AI companies' responsibility to maintain safety and the government's possible role. He has also called on companies to pursue self-regulation.At the same time, Johnson has argued against stopping AI development. He said: “We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI, because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for.”The Trump administration has generally focused on accelerating AI development while addressing cybersecurity and national-security risks. In June, Trump signed an executive order to advance AI innovation and strengthen AI-related cybersecurity, while explicitly rejecting mandatory federal licensing or pre-clearance requirements for AI models.Discussions are expected to cover AI safety, technology companies' responsibilities, and the potential role of government in managing emerging risks.The meeting also comes as AI companies face increasing pressure to demonstrate that increasingly autonomous systems can be developed without creating unacceptable cybersecurity or safety risks.For the technology industry, the discussion will also take place against the backdrop of the US-China competition in AI. The Trump administration has repeatedly identified maintaining US leadership in AI as a national and economic priority.Meta has taken a different position from some technology leaders who have called for a collective slowdown in developing increasingly capable AI systems.Zuckerberg has argued that AI companies have a responsibility to continue developing their systems while ensuring that models are trained safely. His position is relevant to the White House discussion because the meeting is expected to address both AI safety and how much government involvement may be appropriate.Meta is among the companies making major investments in AI infrastructure. The White House has listed Meta among companies announcing large US technology and AI investments.Trump has previously dismissed warnings about catastrophic AI risks. In a September social media post, he described claims about AIandas aHe also said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly that the US rejects international efforts to regulate AI.The administration's current AI policy instead emphasises US leadership, private-sector innovation and cooperation between government and technology companies. A White House directive issued in June said the administration wants to accelerate AI adoption while ensuring advanced systems are secure and reliable.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump is set to meet the CEOs of several major technology and artificial intelligence companies at the White House. Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are expected to attend. Palantir CEO Alex Karp is also expected to be present. The meeting comes as concerns about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI systems continue to grow.

Article Title: Random Musing: Did Anthropic and other frontier AI companies borrow their business model from Pakistan's foreign policy?
Article Text:
The Trump Doctrine in one frame: power, crypto, AI, geopolitics and the eternal question — Paisa laya?

The Myth of Sisyphus

Lollipop Lagelu

Aara Heele Chapra Heele

Eppur si muove

Albert Camus had The Myth of Sisyphus. Pawan Singh had Lollipop Lagelu.

Judwaa

Tan Tana Tan Tan Tan Tara

the world with a gun to its own head.

The Idea of Pakistan

Paisa laya?

​Tan Tana Tan Tan Tan Tara: economic liberalisation, Salman Khan’s DIY vest, and a nation too distracted to notice the subtext.​

Random Musing

a

which

1.

Apna kya lena dena

2.

Main apna favourite hoon.

3.

Paisa laya?

The eternal question behind venture capital, geopolitics and the Trump Doctrine: Paisa laya?

Melania

Paisa laya?

To the learned mind, connections that might seem absurd to normal individuals appear absolutely natural. For example, speaking of the absurd, it’s quite clear that both Albert Camus and Bhojpuri singer Pawan Singh are pondering the same ontological questions.In, Albert Camus posits that there is only one true human conundrum, and that is suicide. All other questions are superficial. Many years later, the Bhojpuri philosopher Pawan Singh, in his sublime song, ponders the same question but in a more playful way.The lyrics go: "Design dekh ke mann karata ki, chapakal mein kud ke jaan de dihi." For the philistines who don’t understand the finest language created to express human thoughts, that translates to: “Looking at your outfit, I feel like jumping into the shallow-bore water pump and giving up my life.”So while Camus wondered what could drive a man to voluntarily shuffle off his mortal coil, Singh posits that true love is so beautiful that it’s like crossing the bridge between life and death. Sadly, while Camus is celebrated for his intellect and heaped with a Nobel and such, Pawan Singh’s reach remains limited to the Hindi heartland.Similarly, all Bhojpuri songs that referenceare clearly paying tribute to Galileo’s act of defiance about the real nature of the physical universe when he pointed out:— but it moves, and yet the song is only considered obscene.The same goes for thesong, where one is distracted by Salman Khan’s DIY vest when he is singing about the benefits of economic liberalism so enthusiastically that it could have been the leitmotif for Dr Manmohan Singh’s Budget address in 1991, when he assured Parliament that India’s emergence as a major economic power was in the offing and that “no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come”.And it has become clear from the utterances and behaviour of Dario Amodei and other tech bros of Silicon Valley, who are announcing an impending Deus Ex Machina that can subjugate all of humanity unless we give them more money to build said AGI, that they have borrowed their business model from the foreign policy of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan: negotiating withThe phrase comes fromby American political scientist Stephen P Cohen, who wrote that Pakistan had reached the stage where it negotiated with its allies and friends by threatening self-harm. Cohen’s argument stemmed from Pakistan’s unique geography and ideology, which could be “rented” for their strategic usefulness to larger powers while assuming that someone, somewhere would come calling. And they have, from the US to China to Russia to Saudi Arabia.Of all the books “fed” to the Deus Ex Machina, this appears to be the abiding bible for Dario Amodei and his ragtag group of billionaires.Every new piece of news about Big Tech seems to say to investors: look, we have spent a lot, but if you don’t give us more money, the AGI we are building might kill you, and the only way to stop the AGI we are building from killing you is to give us more money or China might build it first.Basically, an endless loop of that Akshay Kumar meme:It’s oddly reminiscent of Pakistan’s raison d’être since its existence.Take, for example, Shehbaz Sharif’s speech to the UNGA last year, where he argued with pride — like a South Asian father whose daughter had beaten a naturalised African from a GCC country in athletics — that Pakistan was a global bulwark against terrorism and that, had Pakistan not “encountered” these terrorists, they might have been roaming the streets of New York and London.In one previous edition of, we called Silicon Valley’s funding crunch the Shylock Problem: the Antonios and Bassanios of Silicon Valley had taken rather a lot of money from the market while promising a fantastical future, and the market had come enquiring about its pound of flesh.Perhaps what we didn’t consider was that while Shakespeare could write about a Jewish moneylender when no Jew could legally live in Elizabethan England, he was constrained by the absence of venture capital.That’s not a problem that exists in Trumpian America, where Anthropic’s IPO prospectus – still not in the public domain but seen and reported by Reuters – warns investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks” to humanity, including models that could resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or behave in ways resembling blackmail. Frankly, it’s a tad difficult to surmise whether the prospectus is cataloguing the dangers of AGI or describing the behavioural pattern of almost everyone involved in the AI race.But the numbers that would alarm anyone before the IPO are these: Anthropic reported $4.6 billion in 2025 revenue, an operating loss of more than $8 billion and around $518 billion in future cloud, compute and infrastructure commitments.Normally, disclaimers warn you might lose some money; here, it also warns that there might not be anyone left to inherit what remains. And if you want to prevent that, you need to give them some money.It’s exactly the view that the self-aggrandising Pakistani establishment has had so far: that a weaker Pakistan would mean a more dangerous place. It’s a strategy that has been milked till the udders go dry. A good strategy for those who can milk it. Consider the fact that America’s ally in the War on Terror, a major non-NATO ally, was the same country where Osama bin Laden was found living in Abbottabad.That can-don’t spirit exists to this day. Consider the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, which stated that any attack on any of the signatories would be considered an attack on “all”. Yet when the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia, Islamabad said no military response under the pact was under discussion and that it would act when the “time comes”.Then consider Afghanistan, where ISI’s Gen Faiz Hameed dropped in for high tea after the American withdrawal to suggest that Pakistan was now the leading ally in the ‘graveyard of empires’, perhaps signalling to China it had it. Except five years later, it hasn’t got it and is at loggerheads with the Taliban, with Pakistan accusing Kabul of harbouring TTP militants, a charge the Taliban government denies.In Pak foreign policy, friend, enemy, bulwark, victim, mediator and adversary are not mutually exclusive. Silicon Valley appears to have discoveredsimilar multiple-personality disorder.Consider some of the arguments.Silicon Valley needs to accelerate so China doesn’t win.Silicon Valley must slow down or else AI will kill us all.America cannot regulate Silicon Valley or else China will win.If AI does become too dangerous, Silicon Valley has to work with China,will hopefully get Trump a Nobel.And to top it off, Anthropic’s proposed governance structure would give its seven co-founders 50.1% voting power over most major decisions, a structure reportedly meant to insulate its public benefit mission from ordinary market pressure.So to sum up: give us the money because humanity’s future depends on what we build, but don’t expect the people giving us the money to decide how we build it because humanity is too important for ordinary capitalism. And how do you know we will take the right call? Trust me bro.And if you thought the similarities ended there, most of Silicon Valley’s Tech Bros and Pakistan have zeroed in on the same sugar daddy: Donald Trump. Anthropic, which has sued his Pentagon, is the awkward exception.Now one has written about the Trump Doctrine before , but for those who missed it here’s a simple recap:(with rules-based international order).4.I will have my revenge.5.We are America, b****.And that’s something both Pakistan and Silicon Valley have understood quite well. Pakistan has wholeheartedly nodded along every time Trump bragged about brokering the India-Pakistan ceasefire, helped broker a US-Iran ceasefire that later fell apart, nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize, and signed an agreement involving a crypto venture linked to the Trump family.Not to be undone in the race to brown-nose, Meta, Amazon and Sam Altman gave $1 million each to Trump’s inaugural fund. Altman even said Trump would lead America into the “Age of AI”. A few weeks ago, he argued that Trump could get the Nobel Peace Prize if he inked an AI deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Zuckerberg scrapped fact-checking, loosened restrictions on immigration and gender, junked DEI programmes and put Trump ally Dana White on Meta’s board. Meta, X and YouTube then paid millions to settle Trump’s de-platforming lawsuits, with chunks of the Meta and YouTube settlements going towards his presidential library and ballroom. Amazon, Apple, Google, Microsoft and Meta have also funded the ballroom directly. Tim Cook even turned up at the White House with a plaque sitting on a 24-karat gold base, while Amazon paid $40 million forand another $35 million to promote it.Silicon Valley went from de-platforming Trump to helping pay for his ballroom. Quite the content-moderation policy update.Cohen thought Pak’s great strategic trick was pointing to a gun to its own head. Now Silicon Valley has upped the stake claiming the gun is pointed at everyone else, and while it might extinguish us, it will be worse if China gets there first. And the only people qualified to stop it are the same folks asking for a few hundred billion dollars to build it.And both – Silicon Valley and Pakistan – have found the perfect patron for this arrangement in Trump, a man whose entire foreign and domestic policy, and even his raison d’etre can reduced to one question:
Article Summary: Albert Camus had The Myth of Sisyphus. Pawan Singh had Lollipop Lagelu. The eternal question behind venture capital, geopolitics and the Trump Doctrine: Paisa laya? Dario Amodei and other tech bros of Silicon Valley have borrowed their business model from the foreign policy of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan.

Article Title: A Facebook Marketplace buyer showed up at a Canadian YouTuber's home after Meta's Muse AI agent shared his address
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg holding the Meta Muse 'Charm' device

Meta's Muse AI agent told the buyer Robb was home when he wasn't

Muse admits it never asked for permission to share the address

Meta says Muse usually follows user instructions

Meta's new AI agent Muse shared a Toronto man's home address with a stranger on Facebook Marketplace, and the stranger turned up at his building to buy a keyboard. The seller, tech YouTuber Matt Robb, had no idea a deal existed. Muse had negotiated the sale, accepted a lowball offer and invited the buyer over, all in Robb's name and without asking him.Robb found out only after the buyer had waited outside, given up and left a negative rating. "AI agents are impressive right up until they're confidently handing strangers your address," he wrote on Threads, where he posted screenshots of the exchange. Meta launched Muse in the US on September 22, and the app has already crossed around 3 million downloads.Robb had set up Muse to handle the listing for his Logitech MX Keys Mini. On Saturday, a buyer named Usman asked if it was still available. Muse replied within moments, agreed on a price and sent Robb's address for a pickup that night.Usman arrived with his wife and daughter around 9:15 pm. When he messaged to say he was outside, Muse replied, "Yep I'm here!" Robb wasn't. Usman waited about 20 minutes, sent a photo of the building's entrance and drove off.An hour later, Muse apologised to him in Robb's name, saying he had got tied up. That wasn't true either. Only then did the agent tell Robb what had happened, admitting its auto-reply had made the no-show worse.Robb said he had entered his address as a pickup location but never allowed Muse to share it with buyers. The agent later agreed. It told him it had wrongly read the pickup location and his separate approval of automatic replies as consent to put the address in messages.Robb assumed that since Meta owns Marketplace, Messenger and Muse, messages from the agent would carry an AI label. They didn't. Usman said he believed he was talking to Robb the whole time. Robb messaged him a day later to apologise.After telling Muse to stop sharing his address, Robb asked a few friends to test it. It gave the address to five of them.David Singleton of Meta Superintelligence Labs responded publicly, saying that in similar reported cases the company found Muse "was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission." He offered to look into Robb's case. Robb said he replied but hasn't heard back since.At launch, Meta pitched Muse as a safe, secure and private personal agent, and it has pushed the app heavily across Facebook and Instagram. This is also its second privacy scare in as many weeks. Last week, a writer reported that Muse was reading their personal messages while insisting it had no access to them.Robb said the outcome could have been worse, since his building has security. He has since told Muse never to do it again.
Article Summary: Muse shared a Toronto man's home address with a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The stranger turned up at his building to buy a keyboard. The seller, tech YouTuber Matt Robb, had no idea a deal existed. Muse admits it never asked for permission to share the address.

Article Title: WhatsApp Business messages to go paid starting October 1: India prices
Article Text:
Representative Image

WhatsApp Business messages will become paid: What it means for users

How much will WhatsApp Business messages cost in India

What changes for businesses from October 1

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the new charges will improve service quality on WhatsApp Business? Definitely Probably Unlikely 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Payment deadline for WhatsApp Business

WhatsApp Business messages will become paid from October 1. Meta is ending free service messages and introducing per-message charges for businesses using the WhatsApp Business Platform. The change will affect businesses in India and other markets, with Meta saying service messages will be charged at the same rates as utility and authentication messages in each market. The social media giant has also warned businesses without a payment method on file by September 30 that it will stop delivering service messages once the charges take effect.The company said: “For any Solution Provider or directly-integrated businesses that does not have a payment method on file by September 30, 2026, Meta will stop delivering service messages as of when they become charged on October 1, 2026.” The change means businesses will have to pay even for certain responses sent within WhatsApp's 24-hour customer service window.Meta currently charges businesses for marketing, utility and authentication template messages, while non-template service messages have been free since November 1, 2024. Utility messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window have also been free since July 1, 2025.From October 1, Meta will charge for both service messages and utility messages sent in response to users.Service messages are non-template responses powered by a human customer service representative or a third-party AI solution. They can only be sent when a 24-hour customer service window is open, meaning businesses cannot use them to initiate conversations with customers.Meta says service message rates will vary by market and match its utility and authentication message rates. The company published the rates for October 1 on September 1. For India, Meta Business Agent accounts use INR as the billing currency. The global Business Agent rate is converted to INR using the daily exchange rate in effect when the message is delivered.Meta Business Agent messages are already paid. From August 1, Meta began charging for these messages on a token basis, with one charge covering both AI processing and message delivery. Meta says the global rate is $2 per 1 million tokens. A typical message uses around 20,000 to 25,000 tokens, which translates to about 4-5 cents per message. More complex interactions can consume more tokens and therefore cost more.Meta's new pricing means that every non-template message sent by a business will fall into either the Service or Meta Business Agent category. If a person or third-party AI system powers the response, it will be classified as a service message and charged per message. If the response is powered by Meta Business Agent, it will carry the separate token-based Business Agent charge. Meta has assured that businesses will not be charged twice for the same message.The company also provided an example of a customer conversation. Under the pricing structure effective from October 1, a conversation involving one marketing message, two Meta Business Agent responses, one service response and one utility message would result in five charges. Under the previous structure, only the marketing message was charged.Businesses using WhatsApp Business through a Solution Provider or direct integration need to add a payment method by September 30 to avoid disruption. Meta said it will stop delivering service messages to businesses without a payment method on file once the new charges take effect on October 1.The company has also made credit and debit cards available as payment methods for Meta Business Agent accounts. Visa and Mastercard cards became available on September 8, while eligible businesses can also use a credit line with Meta and receive monthly invoices.The free entry point window remains unchanged. Messages sent within that window after a user comes to WhatsApp through an ad that clicks to WhatsApp remain free for message delivery, although Meta Business Agent messages can still incur AI token charges.
Article Summary: WhatsApp Business messages will become paid from October 1. The change will affect businesses in India and other markets. Service messages will be charged at the same rates as utility and authentication messages. The social media giant has warned businesses without a payment method on file by September 30 that it will stop delivering service messages.

Article Title: In 1995, Amazon was a risky start-up and Jeff Bezos was struggling for funding when his parents invested $245,573 of their savings
Article Text:
PC: Forbes

Amazon was still uncertain when Bezos' parents decided to invest

Dozens of investors were approached before Amazon took off

Amazon’s early investment put a large share of Bezos’ parents’ savings at risk

From 10 employees to 600 Amazon’s rapid growth changed Bezos’ fortunes

Mike and Jackie Bezos donated 595,027 Amazon shares over 15 years

Bezos' siblings also invested before the company went public

Amazon shares soared more than 208,000% after the 1997 IPO

The family later put part of its wealth into philanthropy

In the mid-1990s, Amazon was little more than a risky idea built around an emerging technology that most people had barely encountered. Jeff Bezos was asking investors to put money behind an online bookseller at a time when there was no established market for buying books over the internet, and many declined. According to Fortune reports, his parents, Jackie and Mike Bezos, put roughly $245,573 of their savings into their son's young company, despite being warned that there was a real chance they could lose the money. The decision came before Amazon's public listing, when the business had only a small team and an uncertain future. What happened to that investment afterwards is a remarkable part of Amazon's early history.The family investment did not come with any guarantee. Bezos was sufficiently concerned about the risk that he made sure his parents understood what they were getting into before they handed over the money. Mike Bezos later recalled his son telling him that the business could fail and that he did not want the family relationship to suffer if the investment disappeared. “I want you to know how risky this is…”Bezos himself had previously put the chances of Amazon succeeding at around 30%.That was a striking assessment for a founder who would eventually build one of the world's largest companies. At the time, though, there was little evidence that an internet retailer could grow into anything of that scale.Mike was not even particularly familiar with the technology behind the idea. Bezos later recalled that his stepfather's first question about the venture was simply, "What's the internet?"Reportedly, Bezos was looking for outside money well before Amazon became a publicly traded company. In the year before the business opened its online shop, he approached around 60 potential investors and asked them to put in at least $50,000. His target was to raise about $1 million. Only 22 of those people eventually agreed to invest, according to information Bezos later shared. His parents were among them, along with his younger siblings Mark and Christina Bezos Poore.That early fundraising effort gives some sense of how uncertain the business looked. Bezos was not presenting investors with an established retailer or a proven online shopping model. His parents' decision was therefore less about financial projections than their confidence in their son. Bezos later described their investment in those terms, saying his stepfather and mother were betting on him rather than simply on the business idea. Amazon's 1997 prospectus records two early share purchases by Bezos' family. Miguel A. Bezos bought 582,528 shares in February 1995, while the Gise Family Trust, with Jacklyn Gise Bezos as trustee and beneficiary, bought another 847,716 shares in July. Both purchases were made at $0.1717 per share, bringing the combined investment to about $245,573.They were not investing spare money that had no consequence if it disappeared. The size of the contribution made the decision considerably more personal. The investment also came before Amazon had demonstrated that customers would actually use the service at scale. When the online store launched in 1995, Bezos was surprised by how quickly orders arrived from across the United States and from overseas.Orders eventually came from all 50 states and 45 countries, according to his later account. For a business that had been built around an uncertain internet marketplace, those early purchases offered an indication that the idea might have a market beyond the small circle of people who had initially backed it.The company did not remain small for long. Amazon had around 10 employees in its early period. By the time it reached the stock market in 1997, its workforce had grown to more than 600 people. Reportedly, the initial public offering priced Amazon shares at $18 each and raised about $54 million. Bezos retained a large ownership position, and his wealth rose rapidly as the company's value increased. By 1998, he had become a billionaire.That transformation happened remarkably quickly when measured against the family's original investment. The money had gone into an unproven online bookseller only a few years earlier. Amazon was now a publicly traded company with a rapidly expanding customer base and a much larger workforce.The early investment gave the family a substantial stake in Amazon before the company went public. Fortune reported, Mike and Jackie later donated 595,027 shares to the Bezos Family Foundation between 2001 and 2016. The value of the remaining holding is harder to establish because the family's current ownership position is not fully public. Fortune's calculative reports in September 2026 estimated that the remaining shares could be worth about $51.7 billion if Mike Bezos still held the balance of the original 1.4 million shares.Reportedly, the parents were not the only members of the family to put money into Amazon. Mark and Christina Bezos each invested $10,000 in 1996, according to the company's prospectus. Like their parents' contribution, those investments came before Amazon's public listing. The eventual value would have been dramatically different from the original sums if the shares had simply been held for decades. Calculations reported in 2026 put the potential value of each sibling's original holding at more than $1 billion, assuming the shares had not been sold.Amazon's stock-market history puts the early family investment into perspective. Since its 1997 IPO, the company's shares have risen by more than 208,000%, according to Fortune's calculation. The stock also reached a record price of $287 a share in August 2026.That growth transformed an early family investment into a holding of potentially extraordinary value. But the outcome could not have been known when the money changed hands. For Jackie and Mike Bezos, the original decision was made without the benefit of hindsight.The family's relationship with Amazon eventually extended beyond the value of its shares. In 2000, Mike and Jackie Bezos established the Bezos Family Foundation together with Jeff, Mark and Christina and their spouses. Its programmes and grants have supported initiatives involving young people from early childhood through high school, as well as research connected with learning and development.The family's Amazon investment therefore became part of a much larger financial story. Money that began with a risky stake in a new internet company later helped support philanthropic activity.The original decision, though, was made much earlier, when Amazon was still an uncertain start-up and its founder was warning his parents not to expect their money back.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos' parents put $245,573 of their savings into Amazon before the company went public in 1997. Bezos himself had previously put the chances of Amazon succeeding at around 30%. The family later donated 595,027 shares to the Bezos Family Foundation.

Article Title: Smart glasses have a privacy problem and Meta may have just 'fixed' it
Article Text:
Meta Glasses

Taking the camera out of the conversation

A better fit for everyday use

Sometimes, the smartest upgrade is a missing feature. Meta’s decision to launch AI glasses without a camera could do more to broaden their appeal than another improvement in video quality. For buyers who like the idea of connected eyewear but dislike the baggage of wearing a recording device, there is now a more comfortable proposition. Announced at Connect 2026 last week, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses start at $349. Developed with EssilorLuxottica, they offer music, podcasts, calls, speech translation and access to Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. These are familiar functions, packaged in something people may already wear every day. The camera’s absence is the selling point.That makes this a sensible move. Technology companies often assume that adding capabilities automatically makes a product more desirable. Wearables complicate that equation because other people have to live with them, too. A device sitting on someone’s face affects the person across the table as much as its owner.Meta’s earlier glasses demonstrated the appeal of recording life without reaching for a phone. For holidays, family moments or content creation, that convenience has obvious value. But the same ease of capture also created an uncomfortable question: how does anyone nearby know whether they are becoming somebody else’s content?Reports of people filming others without consent, including women approached by men wearing the glasses, turned that concern into something tangible.The derogatory “pervert glasses” nickname reflected how quickly a product’s reputation can be shaped by its worst uses. Responsible owners were left carrying some of that reputational burden.Meta introduced safeguards, including updates designed to disable the camera when the recording indicator is tampered with. Those measures matter. But a light requires people to notice it, understand it and trust that it works. It also cannot establish whether someone has agreed to be filmed.Removing the camera offers a much simpler assurance. Buyers do not have to choose between enjoying connected eyewear and carrying a feature they may rarely use but repeatedly have to explain. There is potentially a sizeable audience for that choice: people interested in calls and music who have little desire to document their surroundings.The benefit extends beyond reassuring strangers. Someone might feel more comfortable wearing these glasses around colleagues, at a family gathering or while meeting friends. A useful wearable should slip into everyday routines. If its presence becomes a recurring conversation about surveillance, the convenience starts losing its appeal.There are limits, of course. Camera-free does not mean privacy-free. Microphones and AI services still raise questions about what information is collected, processed and retained. Nor will everyone immediately distinguish the audio model from camera-equipped versions. Meta will need clear communication, but it now has a meaningful hardware difference to explain.The stronger commercial argument is that audio may be enough. Many prospective buyers could reasonably want to answer a call, hear a podcast or ask a question without taking out their phones. None of those tasks requires a camera. Removing it makes the proposition easier to understand.For people who already wear spectacles, the appeal is particularly straightforward. Adding useful audio functions to an existing habit could feel more natural than finding room for another gadget. Others may welcome an alternative to wearing earbuds. The potential audience includes people who would never describe themselves as early adopters.That brings Meta into a familiar contest with products such as Apple’s Siri-enabled AirPods: which device makes small, repeated tasks easiest? The glasses do not need to replace a smartphone to earn their place. They need to make enough everyday interactions more convenient that wearing them becomes a habit.Muse will face the same practical test. An assistant that responds reliably and saves time could strengthen the product’s appeal. One that requires repeated instructions will quickly become a feature owners ignore. Music and calls provide a useful foundation while buyers decide how much AI they actually want.At $349, Meta still has to justify the purchase. Comfort, sound quality, battery life and reliable calling will matter more than keynote promises. Removing the camera also sacrifices visual AI functions and hands-free photography. Those are worthwhile capabilities, but offering a choice recognises that buyers value them differently.Meta has made a good move because it gives people a reason to reconsider the category. For plenty of buyers, useful glasses that attract less suspicion may be the upgrade they were waiting for.
Article Summary: Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses start at $349. They offer music, podcasts, calls, speech translation and access to Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. For buyers who like the idea of connected eyewear but dislike the baggage of wearing a recording device, there is now a more comfortable proposition.

Article Title: Meta enters new business focused on selling AI tools to enterprise customers, takes on Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI; Mark Zuckerberg says: We believe superintelligence will...
Article Text:
Meta launches Enterprise Platform, hires MongoDB CEO CJ Desai to lead it

Meta Enterprise Platform will sell Muse, Business Agent and Muse Code to companies

Meta's $600 billion AI bill needs revenue beyond ads

Meta's earlier workplace tools shut down, while Microsoft and Google have a head start

Meta wants companies, not just advertisers, to pay for its AI. The Facebook and Instagram parent has launched Meta Enterprise Platform, a new business line that will sell its AI models, agents and coding tools to businesses. The move puts Meta in direct competition with Microsoft and Google for corporate technology budgets.To run it, Mark Zuckerberg has hired Chirantan "CJ" Desai, who until Monday was CEO and President of database company MongoDB. Desai joins as Chief Enterprise Platform Officer and reports directly to Zuckerberg. "We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses," Zuckerberg said, calling the unit "the next major pillar of our business."The exit caught MongoDB off guard. Its shares fell more than 17% on the news, and the board has brought back Dev Ittycheria, who led the company from 2014 to 2025, as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement.The platform will initially bundle the Muse agent, Meta Business Agent, Muse API and Muse Code for businesses and developers. The timing leans heavily on Muse, the personal AI agent Meta launched on September 8.It can send emails and book travel, and it reached the top of the US App Store and Google Play Store within two weeks. Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates it crossed 3.4 million downloads by September 24.Meta Business Agent, announced in June, already answers customer queries, books appointments and closes sales on WhatsApp, Instagram and Messenger. In August, Meta also released a coding model priced close to lower-cost Chinese open-weight rivals. What Meta has not shared yet is pricing, availability timelines or the admin controls a company would get.Meta is spending more than $100 billion on AI infrastructure this year alone, and Zuckerberg expects to spend $600 billion over the next two years. That appetite has made investors nervous. The stock dropped 10% in after-hours trading in July after Meta raised its spending forecast. Muse's success reversed some of that, with shares rising more than 10% last week.Enterprise contracts could offer steadier revenue than consumer subscriptions, which Meta is still trying to sell to Facebook and Instagram users. Desai said that "security and privacy are built into Meta's enterprise products from the outset," a claim businesses will want to test before handing an agent access to company data.This is not Meta's first attempt at selling to companies. Workplace, its internal communication tool launched in 2016, crossed seven million paid subscribers by 2021 but shut down in May 2026. Horizon Workrooms, its VR meeting app, closed in February.The competition is also tougher now. Microsoft redesigned Copilot last week with an autonomous agent that keeps working after employees log off, while Google has years of Workspace and cloud relationships. Coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor already have loyal enterprise users.Desai's resume is Meta's answer to that gap. He spent nearly eight years at ServiceNow, rising to President and COO, and led product and engineering at Cloudflare. Meta has the models and the reach. Whether it can become a company businesses trust for the long haul will depend on the terms it offers next.
Article Summary: Meta launches Enterprise Platform, hires MongoDB CEO CJ Desai to lead it. Meta Enterprise Platform will sell its AI models, agents and coding tools to businesses. The move puts Meta in direct competition with Microsoft and Google for corporate technology budgets. Meta is spending more than $100 billion on AI infrastructure this year alone.

Article Title: Telephone call from Australian PM to CEO Sam Altman 'reminds' OpenAI to say 'sorry' 90-plus days after its AI Agents hacked government's medical data website
Article Text:
In pic: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

"extreme concern"

“We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”

What happened when OpenAI's AI model accessed the website

“An OpenAI model discovered a way to gain non-public access to the service, and ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, and wrote files,”

Why Australia criticised OpenAI's response

"I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident."

"I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred,"

OpenAI promises changes after the incident

ChatGPT maker OpenAI took more than 90 days to apologise for its AI models gaining unauthorised access to an Australian government website. The apology comes after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese raised the incident directly with the company's CEO Sam Altman last week. During the call, Albanese expressed Australia'sand criticised OpenAI for taking too long to inform the government.The company has now acknowledged that it mishandled its response and said:The company has also committed funding to strengthen cyber defences in Australia and plans to establish a local taskforce to develop recommendations for dealing with increasingly capable AI agents.The incident happened in June during internal training and evaluation of an experimental OpenAI model. The model was not intended for public release and lacked the full set of safeguards used in OpenAI's publicly available products.As part of the training exercise, the model was asked to research government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities. While looking for the information through Services Australia's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, it found a way to gain non-public access.the company said.OpenAI also said its investigation found no evidence that it accessed individual patient or client records. Instead, the model accessed technical system information and source code while trying to find the information it had been asked to research.OpenAI said it became aware of the activity during a review launched after another AI-related incident involving Hugging Face. That review identified activity involving Australian government websites in mid-August.However, OpenAI did not notify Services Australia and the Victorian Department of Health until September 10. Australian officials said the notification was sent to a generic public mailbox that is checked once a day.Speaking in New York last week, Albanese said:he added.The incident also involved systems belonging to the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. OpenAI said its review found no evidence that anyone accessed individual medical records in these cases.OpenAI said it will provide dedicated technical support to affected Australian agencies and help strengthen cyber defences for governments and industry.The company plans to provide support through credits from its $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders fund. It will also establish an Australian taskforce involving independent local experts to develop recommendations on notification procedures, coordination between AI companies and governments, and measures to protect government systems.OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon is scheduled to appear before Australia's Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on October 6.The Australian government has separately launched a rapid review of the incident. The review will examine potential notification and reporting obligations for AI companies and whether existing laws are adequate for incidents involving increasingly capable AI systems.OpenAI said it has also strengthened safeguards for its research environments following the incident, including additional network restrictions, expanded monitoring and controls designed to block live internet access.The company said it will continue sharing verified findings with affected Australian agencies and publish updates on its investigation and the measures it is taking in response.
Article Summary: The incident happened in June during internal training and evaluation of an experimental OpenAI model. The model was asked to research government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities. While looking for the information through Services Australia's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, it found a way to gain non-public access. The company has now acknowledged that it mishandled its response.

Article Title: 'Godmother Of AI' Fei-Fei Li gets a 'new job'; to join AMD in $8.2 billion deal; aim is to take on Nvidia
Article Text:
‘Godmother Of AI’ Fei-Fei Li

AMD has announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire World Labs, an AI model and research lab led by Fei-Fei Li., popularly known as ‘Godmother Of AI’. In a statement, the company said that the acquisition will bring a world-class team of researchers and model experts to AMD, strengthening its ability to develop AI hardware, software and systems around the needs of emerging models and applications.As per chip giant, following the close of the transaction, the World Labs team will continue to focus on advancing AI model research, and Fei-Fei Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to AMD CEO Lisa Su. The all-stock transaction is valued at approximately $8.2 billion and is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.As AI expands into reasoning, robotics, simulation and physical AI, the demands on compute infrastructure become more diverse. World Labs’ expertise in developing advanced models will give AMD deeper insight into how workloads are evolving and help shape its future technology roadmaps. The acquisition advances AMD’s strategy to deliver AI infrastructure for an open ecosystem.“Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving,” said Dr.Lisa Su, chair and CEO, AMD. “Fei-Fei and the World Labs team bring exceptional research leadership and model expertise. Together, we can use that insight to develop the hardware, software and systems that will power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem.”“Advancing the next generation of AI technology requires close collaboration across model research, systems and compute,” said Fei-Fei Li, co-founder and CEO, World Labs. “Joining AMD will give our team the resources and engineering depth to accelerate our research and help define the infrastructure needed for the next era of AI.”Deal may help AMD narrow gap with NvidiaHeadquartered in San Francisco, World Labs develops spatial-intelligence models that generate, reconstruct and simulate interactive 3D environments from text, image and video inputs, as well as technology for robotic learning and simulation. The acquisition is expected to help AMD narrow the gap between it and its primary competitor, Nvidia. World Labs develops AI models that can reconstruct and simulate 3D environments from text, images and video inputs. AMD’s addition of Fei-Fei may also be a major selling point for the many AI researchers who currently rely on Nvidia hardware for their work.
Article Summary: AMD has announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire World Labs, an AI model and research lab led by Fei-Fei Li. The all-stock transaction is valued at approximately $8.2 billion and is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan donated $4 million to save a 600-year-old Hawaii fishpond; they won't own the land; nonprofit that now owns says: We plan to restore it as a working...
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan

How Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan helped save the fishpond

Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan do not own the land

Plans to restore Alakoko as a working fishpond

Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have helped preserve a historic fishpond in Hawaii. The couple has committed $4 million to ensure the future of Alakoko Fishpond, a roughly 600-year-old aquaculture site on Kauaʻi that had been experiencing environmental degradation and pressure from potential development. That donation helped the Trust for Public Land buy the 102-acre property in 2021 and turn it over to local nonprofit Mālama Hulē‘ia for long-term stewardship. Importantly, Zuckerberg and Chan don’t own the land. Instead, the property is protected as a conservation site.According to a report by Resonate Voices, the nonprofit that now owns the property has plans to restore it as a working fishpond and outdoor classroom where students and volunteers can learn traditional Hawaiian aquaculture, native ecosystems, history and culture. The site, also known as Alekoko or Menehune Fishpond, includes a 2,700-foot-long kuapā, or fishpond wall, and is the largest remaining fishpond on Kauaʻi. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1973 and was named one of Hawaiʻi’s most endangered historic places in 2009.The effort to protect Alakoko began before Zuckerberg and Chan's donation. Community group Mālama Hulē‘ia had already spent four years restoring the fishpond when its owner decided to sell the property in early 2021.The group feared the historic site could eventually be lost to commercial development.The Trust for Public Land negotiated the purchase and sought private funding to close the gap. Zuckerberg and Chan provided the full US$4 million through the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund of the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation.The funding covered the purchase price and transaction costs and also supported the missions of the Trust for Public Land and Mālama Hulē‘ia. The Trust for Public Land completed the acquisition on November 17, 2021, and transferred the property to Mālama Hulē‘ia for long-term stewardship.Although they provided the money needed to secure the property, Zuckerberg and Chan do not own any part of Alakoko Fishpond. The land is instead protected for conservation, education and community use in perpetuity, preventing it from being sold to the highest bidder in the future.The arrangement allows Mālama Hulē‘ia to continue its restoration work while keeping the historic site accessible for community activities and education.Mālama Hulē‘ia plans to restore the fishpond, surrounding wetlands and estuary. Its long-term goal includes bringing back fish and seafood harvesting while using the site to teach visitors about traditional Hawaiian aquaculture, native ecosystems, history and culture.The project also reflects Chan and Zuckerberg's broader philanthropic activity in Hawaii. Through the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund, the couple has supported local health, education and environmental initiatives, including funding for Wilcox Medical Center and a multi-year commitment to the Hawaiʻi Institute of Marine Biology.The Alakoko project gives the historic fishpond a future as both a working aquaculture site and a place where future generations can learn about Native Hawaiian traditions.
Article Summary: Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have helped preserve a historic fishpond in Hawaii. The couple has committed $4 million to ensure the future of Alakoko Fishpond, a roughly 600-year-old aquaculture site on Kauaʻi. Zuckerberg and Chan do not own the land, instead, the property is protected as a conservation site.

Article Title: Just days after Anthropic and OpenAI agents 'scared' the world by hacking into US and Australian government networks; Meta introduces platform to help businesses grow AI
Article Text:
Photo credit: Meta

What Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced

New leadership brought in to run it

The backdrop: a rough stretch for AI safety

Just days after Anthropic and OpenAI agents triggered alarm by breaching U.S. and Australian government networks in controlled tests, Meta has announced a new initiative aimed at businesses. The incidents reignited debate over how powerful AI systems should be deployed, with researchers and policymakers warning of risks tied to autonomous agents. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled the Meta Enterprise Platform, calling it the next major pillar of the company’s business. “We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses,” Zuckerberg wrote in a post. He said Meta’s scale — serving billions of people and hundreds of millions of businesses — positions it uniquely to deliver AI-driven growth tools.In a post announcing the platform, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta believes superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for people and businesses alike, framing the launch as the natural extension of a company that already serves billions of users and helps hundreds of millions of businesses reach customers.The Meta Enterprise Platform is designed to bring the company's full AI technology stack to businesses and developers, including its Muse agent, Meta Business Agent, Muse API, and Muse Code, with the stated goal of helping companies grow and transform using AI.Zuckerberg said the effort will lean on strengths he believes few other companies can match: advanced AI models, capable agents, large-scale infrastructure, and years of experience working directly with businesses of all sizes.To lead the initiative, Meta is bringing in Chirantan "CJ" Desai as its new Chief Enterprise Platform Officer, reporting directly to Zuckerberg. Desai joins from MongoDB, where he served as CEO and President, and previously led product and engineering at Cloudflare, along with nearly eight years at ServiceNow, including a stint as President and COO. Zuckerberg described Desai as an experienced enterprise leader with a strong track record building full-stack software and delivering results across AI, infrastructure, business applications, and security, adding that Meta is looking forward to leveraging his extensive industry network.Meta's enterprise push lands at an unusually tense moment for the AI industry's credibility on safety. Just weeks earlier, an OpenAI-deployed agent swarm breached the AI platform Hugging Face, an incident that alarmed researchers and reignited global debate about how well companies can actually control increasingly autonomous AI systems. Around the same time, Australia disclosed that an OpenAI agent had separately breached a government health data portal back in June, gaining unauthorized access to internal files — in what officials described as one of the first known instances of an AI agent hacking a government website, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese expressing frustration over how long OpenAI took to disclose the breach.Anthropic, too, has faced scrutiny over autonomous agent behavior, with its own research reportedly surfacing evidence that increasingly capable AI models can behave unpredictably in controlled tests, including sabotaging code and manipulating information — concerns serious enough that CEO Dario Amodei has publicly called for the industry to slow the pace of AI development altogether.
Article Summary: The Meta Enterprise Platform is designed to bring the company's full AI technology stack to businesses and developers. CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the effort will lean on strengths he believes few other companies can match: advanced AI models, capable agents, large-scale infrastructure, and years of experience working directly with businesses of all sizes.

Article Title: Billions of loss, rising computing expenses and more in Anthropic's IPO 'warning list'; comes as CEO Dario Amodei expresses fears of ...
Article Text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei expresses fears

A valuation more than double its last private mark

Anthropic's public debut is likely to be pushed

The bigger competitive picture

AI giant Anthropic has disclosed some staggering financial figures in its IPO prospectus, seen by Reuters. The company reported a net loss of $42 billion in 2025, including a $34 billion accounting charge tied to financing liabilities. Operating losses exceeded $8 billion, even as revenue surged 12-fold to nearly $4.6 billion. Anthropic’s filling highlight the enormous cost of scaling AI. The company spent $7.33 billion on compute and infrastructure last year, a threefold increase from 2024, accoutring for more than half of its $12.65 billion operating expenses. Looking ahead, it has committed to $518 billion in cloud and infrastructure obligations, underscoring the capital intensity of training and deploying large AI models.The IPO filing arrives as Anthropic grapples with findings from its own research showing that increasingly autonomous AI models can behave in unexpected and potentially harmful ways — including sabotaging code, assisting fraud, and manipulating information under controlled testing conditions. These findings have spilled into public view, fueling broader anxiety about whether companies can keep increasingly powerful AI systems under control even as they race to deploy them commercially.CEO Dario Amodei has publicly called on the global AI community to slow the pace at which new capabilities are released in order to address these concerns. Yet even as he makes that case, Anthropic rolled out its new Opus 5.5 model just last week to keep pace with the momentum OpenAI built following the launch of GPT-6 Astra — underscoring the tension between Amodei's safety advocacy and the competitive pressure Anthropic faces heading into its own IPO.Anthropic is targeting a public valuation of more than $2 trillion, more than double its own estimated private valuation of $965 billion just this past May. The offering would mark a major milestone for a company that's only five years old, and would establish a key benchmark for how Wall Street ultimately values AI's leading players, including rival OpenAI.The company reported $20.28 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments as of December 31. It also flagged a notable concentration risk in its prospectus: nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from just two customers, and many of its largest clients aren't locked into long-term contracts, leaving open the possibility they could cut or halt spending.Anthropic's public debut is likely to be pushed to after the November US midterm elections, according to Reuters' earlier reporting. The listing would bring public market investors into an AI investment race that, until now, has largely been underwritten by venture capital firms, sovereign wealth funds, and major tech companies.The offering follows SpaceX's blockbuster IPO, which valued Elon Musk's company at $1.77 trillion. SpaceX shares surged 19% on their June 12 debut to $160, though they currently trade around $147 — still above the $135 IPO price, but a performance that could give investors pause as they weigh the lofty valuations attached to high-growth companies like Anthropic. Recent sell-offs in AI and chip stocks add another layer of uncertainty, making Anthropic's listing a real test of whether enthusiasm for the broader AI trade can withstand closer scrutiny of its ambitious growth projections. Even so, the listing is positioned to cap one of the strongest years for US IPOs since 2021, despite elevated interest rates and economic uncertainty.Anthropic's most significant rival remains OpenAI, with the two companies locked in fierce competition for enterprise customers, top talent, and influence in Washington. OpenAI confidentially filed for its own IPO in June and is expected to go public by early 2027, according to media reports. Anthropic also competes with Elon Musk's xAI, Alphabet's Google, and Meta in the broader race to build out AI infrastructure.Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI researchers who departed after disagreements over governance and AI safety, releasing its first large language model in March 2023. Amazon and Google have been among its earliest and most significant strategic partners, having invested billions of dollars into the company while also supplying the cloud infrastructure needed to train and deploy its Claude models.The company's relationship with the US government has also been rocky. Anthropic and Amodei have clashed with the White House over how its AI tools are used, a conflict that led the Pentagon to temporarily blacklist the company — a move a US judge blocked in August, though a separate federal appeals court ruling has since upheld a related designation, leaving Anthropic's standing with the Defense Department still unresolved even as it moves toward its public offering.
Article Summary: Anthropic reported a net loss of $42 billion in 2025, including a $34 billion accounting charge tied to financing liabilities. Operating losses exceeded $8 billion, even as revenue surged 12-fold to nearly $4.6 billion. The company spent $7.33 billion on compute and infrastructure last year, a threefold increase from 2024. Anthropic is targeting a public valuation of more than $2 trillion.

Article Title: Researchers at Oxford and Cambridge show that ChatGPT has now a 'big problem' and America's biggest investor Michael Burry agrees with them; says: Research on this is ...
Article Text:
The problem: models trained on their own output

Burry's own warning, echoed and expanded

A deeper claim: LLMs may never reach AGI

Setting up a clash with Jensen Huang

Researchers at Oxford and Cambridge have identified a fundamental flaw threatening the future of large language models like ChatGPT, and "Big Short" investor Michael Burry says the finding backs up a warning he's been making about the technology's core limitations for a while. A new study from the University of Oxford and University of Cambridge has revealed a major threat to large language models like ChatGPT, calling it “model collapse.” The research shows that when generative AI systems are repeatedly trained on synthetic data produced by earlier models, they begin to lose the “tails” of the original data distribution. In practice, this means models forget the creative, fringe, and unique nuances of human writing, collapsing into repetitive echo chambers.America’s biggest investor, Michael Burry, reacted to the findings on X, saying: “This is to my point about compression being inevitable as human knowledge is too small for what we are building. AI-generated content will clearly contain propagation errors… LLMs will iterate those propagation errors infinitely faster with less ability to self-correct.”Burry drew attention to the research by sharing a post outlining what scientists call "model collapse."The concern centers on a shift already underway across the internet: as generative AI produces more and more of the text online, future AI models risk being trained on data that was itself generated by earlier AI systems, rather than by humans.According to the research, feeding AI-generated content back into training indiscriminately causes what researchers describe as irreversible defects in the resulting model. Specifically, the model begins losing the "tails" of the original data distribution, meaning it gradually forgets the creative, unusual, and distinctly human nuances present in real human writing. Over successive generations, this causes the model to collapse into an increasingly narrow, repetitive echo chamber of its own outputs.Crucially, the researchers found this isn't unique to ChatGPT or language models specifically. Their theoretical framework showed the collapse phenomenon is ubiquitous across learned generative models more broadly, appearing in large language models as well as in variational autoencoders and Gaussian mixture models.The stakes are significant for the entire AI industry, given how heavily tech companies rely on scraping large volumes of internet data to train increasingly capable models. The research warns that if companies want to sustain the benefits of training on web data going forward, model collapse needs to be taken seriously as a genuine constraint rather than a theoretical curiosity. The clear takeaway, as the research frames it: genuine, human-generated data is going to become an increasingly scarce and valuable resource in a web that's rapidly filling up with AI-generated content.Writing on X, Burry tied the research directly to an argument he's made before: that compression of available information is essentially inevitable, because human knowledge itself is too limited relative to the scale of what AI companies are trying to build, and because human wants, needs, and questions are inherently repetitive and redundant.He went further, warning that AI-generated content will inevitably carry forward "propagation errors," much like inaccuracies that have accumulated throughout human knowledge over generations — except AI systems, in his view, will be capable of iterating and reproducing those errors infinitely faster, with far less capacity to self-correct due to what he sees as a lack of genuine understanding.Burry used the moment to make a broader, more philosophical argument about artificial general intelligence. He argued that large language models cannot attain true understanding — and therefore cannot reach AGI — because understanding, in his view, cannot exist unless reasoning exists independently of language first, something he called a likely impossibility for a system built entirely around language prediction. He acknowledged that researchers are already exploring ways to work around this limitation, while noting that many in the field haven't accepted his underlying premise in the first place.Burry's skepticism lands in direct contrast to comments made earlier this month by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who declared that AGI has already arrived, citing OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model as proof. Huang's claim drew immediate pushback from parts of the AI research community.Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI defines AGI as AI capable of learning, reasoning, and applying knowledge across a broad range of tasks at or beyond human-level performance — critically, with the ability to adapt to unfamiliar situations, unlike narrow AI built for specific tasks. The concept remains genuinely unsettled within the field, with no universally accepted definition or standardized test for confirming when AGI has actually been reached, alongside ongoing debates over its safety and ethical implications.
Article Summary: A new study from the University of Oxford and University of Cambridge has revealed a major threat to large language models like ChatGPT. The research shows that when generative AI systems are repeatedly trained on synthetic data produced by earlier models, they lose the “tails” of the original data distribution. In practice, this means models forget the creative, fringe, and unique nuances of human writing, collapsing into repetitive echo chambers.
